options: Predisposing
Precipitating
Perpetuating
Protective
questions.explain: Why: in the 4-P grid, protective factors are the patient's strengths and supports — a supportive relative, education and occupational skills, employment and connection with healthcare are the standard social-column protective entries. Not the others: predisposing factors are longstanding vulnerabilities that pre-date the presentation; precipitating factors are the triggers for this episode; perpetuating factors are what maintains the symptoms now, such as housing instability or ongoing legal uncertainty.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with a known personality disorder is medically cleared in the emergency department after a superficial laceration to his forearm. The emergency physician asks the on-call team to admit him. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit him, because self-harm has occurred
Advise that admission is unlikely to help patients with his diagnosis
Assess his current mental state and suicidality
Discharge him with an outpatient psychiatry referral
questions.explain: Why: after medical stabilization, psychiatric assessment must establish the current mental state and risk of suicidality; every disposition decision follows from that assessment. Not the others: automatic admission, automatic discharge and dismissing the admission request are all described as inappropriate without assessment. The second option is a half-truth trap: the teaching point about chronic fluctuating suicidal ideation and admission is real, but stating it before assessing is the error. Note too that deliberate self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent — believe the patient's account of intent and still assess risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman describes three weeks of low mood and poor sleep since her mother's death. She continues to work, manages the household, and her relationships are unchanged; she says she feels sad but that it comes and goes and she can be distracted by her grandchildren. Which feature would most strongly support calling this a mental disorder rather than a normal response?
options: The presence of a clear precipitating stressor
Symptoms persisting beyond two weeks
Clinically significant impairment of her day-to-day functioning
A previous episode of an anxiety disorder in her twenties
questions.explain: Why: a mental disorder involves clinically significant disturbance with functional impairment, and that is the key distinguishing feature from a normal emotional response — here it is exactly what is absent. Not the others: a precipitating stressor does not by itself establish disorder (and the definition excludes an expectable or culturally approved response to a loss); duration alone does not; and a comorbid or past history is not a criterion. This is also why the CS2 history makes impact on day-to-day function at work and at home a core severity domain.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman who recently migrated presents with insomnia and intrusive memories. She tells you, through her teenage son who is interpreting, that she believes her symptoms are a punishment sent by her late grandmother. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Explain that this belief is a symptom and offer psychoeducation to correct it
Arrange a trained interpreter and explore what she thinks is happening
Start an antidepressant immediately and review in six weeks
Reassure her the symptoms will settle and diagnose PTSD
questions.explain: Why: two rules apply at once. Use trained interpreters, not family — a teenage son interpreting for his mother about trauma is exactly the situation the rule addresses. And explore the explanatory model ("What do you think is happening?"), which builds trust and informs culturally sensitive care. Not the others: challenging cultural beliefs is the direct opposite of exploring the explanatory model; starting medication before engagement skips the negotiation the patient has not yet been invited into; and reassurance plus a label neither engages her model nor addresses the interpreter problem.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student reports two months of anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration and fatigue. She has failed two courses and stopped seeing friends. She meets four of the nine DSM criteria for a major depressive episode, so the diagnosis is not made. Which limitation of the DSM system does this best illustrate?
options: Comorbidity produces multiple overlapping labels
Arbitrary diagnostic thresholds exclude clinically significant cases
Dimensional models are too rigid to capture symptom clusters
Heterogeneity means two patients with the same diagnosis differ
questions.explain: Why: the categorical approach can miss meaningful distress and impairment when the symptom count falls just below threshold — 4 of 9 is not an MDE while 5 of 9 is, which is the lecture's own worked illustration. Not the others: comorbidity and heterogeneity are also listed limitations of categorical systems, but neither is what this vignette shows; and the third option inverts the models, since it is categorical rather than dimensional systems that are rigid. The four listed limitations are arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity and subthreshold illness.

guide.s: what you see in their face

cards.prompt: On the MSE, what is the difference between mood and affect, and by which three descriptors is affect described?
cards.answer: Mood is what the patient says — their reply when you ask how their mood is. Affect is what you see in their face as an expression of internal feeling state. Describe the affect, the range, and its appropriateness to content.

guide.s: in the absence of any obvious stimulus

cards.prompt: Define hallucination and illusion, and give the source's example of each.
cards.answer: Hallucination = a sensory experience perceived in the absence of any obvious stimulus (hearing voices with no auditory input). Illusion = misperceiving an existing stimulus as something else (hearing your name called when your phone rings).

guide.s: Both insight and judgment are required to have capacity

cards.prompt: What are the three tasks that make up insight, how does judgment differ, and what do the two together determine?
cards.answer: Insight: (1) accurately recognize new or unusual symptoms; (2) accurately identify them as due to a specific pathological process; (3) accurately recognize the benefits of treatment. Judgment is using that insight to make decisions in one's best interest. Both are required to have capacity to make decisions in one's medical care.

cards.text: Social scientists found inter-rater reliability in psychiatric diagnosis was very low — as low as {{30%}} — and the St. Louis group's symptom-based checklists were developed by {{1972}}.

Freud published his comparison of hysterical versus stroke-related paralysis in {{1893}}, and with Josef Breuer published Studies on Hysteria in {{1895}} — the point at which treatment re-entered psychiatry.

cards.prompt: Define dermatome and myotome as PW02 does.
cards.answer: Dermatome = the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres contained within a single spinal nerve, and therefore arising from a single spinal level. Myotome = the group of muscle cells controlled by the somatic motor fibres within a single spinal nerve; these cells may be distributed into several muscles and can control one or more movements.

cards.answer: Low back pain, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, and bladder and/or bowel dysfunction (urinary retention or overflow, unrecognized fecal incontinence) — with or without lower limb pain, sensory loss or weakness. It is a CORE Back Tool red flag and a surgical emergency; bladder and bowel compromise is a surgical emergency whether the lesion is cord or root.

guide.s: a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness

cards.prompt: Can a cervical lesion cause leg weakness, and what determines the answer?
cards.answer: A cervical spinal cord lesion can, because it affects the upper motor neuron limb of the pathway to the leg. A cervical nerve root lesion cannot. UMN signs (increased tone, brisk reflexes with clonus, extensor plantar) point to the cord and should redirect imaging from the lumbar to the cervical or thoracic spine.

cards.answer: An interaction of genetic predisposition and environmental influences; psychotherapy is the mainstay, and no medication is approved to treat a PD directly.

cards.prompt: Which schizophrenia domain does each Cluster A personality disorder resemble?
cards.answer: Schizotypal resembles positive symptoms, schizoid the negative symptoms, and paranoid PD the paranoid delusions — but with no true hallucinations or delusions.

cards.prompt: What is the "wanting" test for schizoid versus avoidant PD?
cards.answer: Schizoid patients do not want relationships; avoidant patients want them but fear rejection.

cards.prompt: Define validation and invalidation as the module uses them.
cards.answer: Validation is showing you understand someone's experience; invalidation is not understanding it — dismissing, ignoring, not responding, being confused or criticizing.

cards.prompt: What are the four consequences of repeatedly invalidating an emotionally intense person?
cards.answer: Emotions intensify; the sense of self becomes confused; emotions become hard to interpret (alexithymia); emotions become so overwhelming the person seeks escape.

cards.prompt: How long does BPD's affective instability last, and what triggers it?
cards.answer: A few hours to a few days — the module's interview guide says minutes to hours — and it is reactive to external events, unlike a mood episode lasting weeks.

cards.prompt: What is the rationale for restricting access to means, and what should be prescribed?
cards.answer: If a person has to wait, think or problem-solve, the urge may pass before they act. Prescribe small supplies of 1–2 weeks, ask about stockpiling and adherence, and ask about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen and other people's medications.

cards.prompt: On the interview road map, which mental-state section pairs with the history area "emotions"?

cards.prompt: Define mood and affect as the CS2 guide does.
cards.answer: Mood is subjective, reported by the patient (0–10, 0 = worst); affect is objective, observed by the interviewer (quality, intensity, range, stability, congruence).

cards.prompt: Insight versus judgment, and how are they graded?
cards.answer: Insight = realizing you have a mental health concern and appreciating its implications. Judgment = recent behaviours regarding safety, social functioning and treatment decisions. Both graded none/impaired · partial · intact/full.

cards.prompt: What three things must a management plan be, per the CS2 guide?

cards.prompt: The 23-year-old with one-hour episodes of sadness once or twice weekly: on which two grounds did she fail MDE criteria?
cards.answer: (1) No functional impairment — she does not miss work or social events; (2) failure of the duration requirement — a depressive episode needs 2 weeks of symptoms most of the day, nearly every day.

cards.prompt: Harlow gave infant rhesus monkeys a wire mother with milk and a cloth mother without. What was the result, and what does it show?
cards.answer: The infant spent most of its time with the cloth mother, returning to the wire mother only briefly to feed — contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment.

cards.prompt: Which substances can kill you in withdrawal, what do they cause, and what is the named management?
cards.answer: CNS depressants — alcohol, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital — can cause seizures, delirium tremens and death. Management named: diazepam plus thiamine, with admission for IV treatment. Opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but not lethal.

cards.prompt: After a frightening or traumatic event, what proportion of people still have post-traumatic symptoms at one year, and why does that matter?
cards.answer: About 10% — in 90% the symptoms have resolved by a year out. Post-traumatic symptoms are the norm after trauma; it is their persistence in the ~10% minority that constitutes PTSD.

guides.title: Week 40 · 1 Introduction to Psychiatry & the History of Psychiatry
guides.html:
PW01 · PW03 · Foundations

Introduction to Psychiatry & the History of Psychiatry

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The orientation reading's framing, statistics and mental status vocabulary, then Garcia's history module from ancient Egypt to the three rules of DSM-III.

How psychiatry is framed

  • This content is directly referenced and built upon in clerkship — foundational, not a survey course.
  • Medications are paired with the neurobiology of mental illness through interventions such as neurostimulation; even simple behavioural techniques work, alongside a trusting relationship and a little education.
  • The anti-dualism line of the week: the Cartesian split of mind and body "was only ever an illusion".
  • The physician's roles. Beyond medical expert, the psychiatrist must be a skilled communicator, collaborator, manager, and — "perhaps most crucially" — advocate. Note the hedge: advocacy is not ranked outright above the rest.
  • Three student worries are named and answered: Will you be safe? Will the patients and their families be nice? Will anyone ever get better? Yes, as often as in any other area of medicine — but everyone will struggle to believe that at first, because of the stigma these disorders carry. The closing instruction is be kind, be mindful, and be curious.

Five Canadian statistics

#Statistic
1One in three Canadians will experience a mental illness or substance use disorder in their lifetime.
2By age 40, about 50% of the population will have or have had a mental illness.
3More than 10 Canadians die by suicide each day.
4Suicide accounts for 24% of all deaths among 15–24 year olds and 16% among 25–44 year olds.
5Suicide rates among Indigenous youth are among the highest in the world.

Statistic 4 carries two different denominators — 24% of all deaths in the 15–24 band, 16% in the 25–44 band. Neither is a population rate.

The mental status examination

The MSE is psychiatry's physical examination. It formalizes something you have done since infancy — reading verbal and non-verbal cues — and is a cornerstone of a thorough psychiatric assessment. You track and evaluate these signs while you are interviewing the patient, not afterwards.

DomainWhat it is
AppearanceBody habitus, grooming, dress — "well groomed, appropriately dressed" vs "dishevelled, barefoot despite winter weather"
AttitudeThe patient's demeanour — pleasant and engageable vs guarded and irritable
Level of arousalAlert? Somnolent but rousable? Unconscious? If drowsy, are they oriented?
Level of activityNormal speed of motion? Fidgety = psychomotor restlessness; sluggish = psychomotor retardation
MoodWhat the patient says when you ask about their mood — subjective, reported
AffectWhat you see in their face as an expression of internal feeling — describe the affect, its range, and its appropriateness to content ("sad, restricted, appropriate" vs "euphoric, labile, inappropriate")
Thought processOrganization and clarity; normal is goal-directed and logical
SpeechVolume, rate, rhythm and prosody — prosody being sarcastic, earnest, uncertain
Thought contentDelusions (fixed, false beliefs), thoughts of self-harm, of suicide, of harm to others
PerceptionsHallucinations and illusions
CognitionAny cognitive impairment? Screen with the MoCA, or the MMSE — better known, but maybe less reliable
Insight and judgmentSeem intuitive, but are actually complex

Beyond discrete symptoms, look for trends or qualities in a person's thinking that speak to risk: a depressed patient with a poor sense of the future, or one whose paranoid delusions focus on a specific person (a spouse, a boss). Both raise the risk of harm to self or others.

Perceptions — the pair to keep straight
Hallucination = a sensory experience perceived in the absence of any obvious stimulus (hearing voices while there is no auditory input). Illusion = misperceiving a real stimulus as something else (hearing your name called when your phone rings). Commonest in psychosis, but also seen in mood disorders, delirium and temporal lobe epilepsy.

Insight is three separate tasks: (1) accurately recognize new or unusual symptoms ("I'm much more sad and hopeless than usual"); (2) accurately identify them as a specific pathological process ("I am having a depressive episode"); (3) accurately recognize the benefits of treatment ("restarting my antidepressant would help"). Judgment is the ability to use insight to make decisions in your own best interest. The examinable link: both insight and judgment are required to have capacity to make decisions about your medical care. Assessing either is difficult, especially once clinician bias is factored in.

The history of psychiatry

The discipline moves as a chain of matched hopes and disappointments: a unifying explanation is adopted, over-applied, then corrected. Four forces run underneath the whole story.

Four background forces
1. Eugenics — degeneration, and the belief that "devolving" people could be identified by physical characteristics. 2. Colonialism — asylums built across the UK and its colonies, especially the US and Canada, drawing on the biramistan model from Middle Eastern medicine. 3. Militarization of medicine — shell shock, and returning soldiers to the battlefield. 4. Unification vs pluralism — the pull between one explanation and many. Watch for these working in the background of every era below.
  • Ancient Egypt. Two scrolls reference mood and psychotic symptoms, and give the first description of the "wandering uterus" — the origin of hysteria, and it belongs to Egypt, not Greece. There is no association with the brain at all; treatment is spiritual and magical.
  • Ancient Greece. Hippocratic writings recognize melancholia, psychosis and mania. Everything is about the humours. Management is already biopsychosocial in shape, while treatment is the science of the time — bloodletting and the like.
  • Medieval Europe. Illness is either dangerous immoral forces (witchcraft, possession) or an imbalance of humours. Institutionalization begins in the late 1400s, but often not separate from the carceral system — an entanglement the story returns to at the very end.

Each era: a hope and a disappointment

EraThe hopeThe disappointment
The asylum
1600s–1890s		Funded places from the early 1600s for safety and a humane alternative to jail or homelessness; later the architecture, grounds, institutional rules and daily work were themselves thought curative. Peak in 1850s England.Scandals of poor care and unexplained deaths; a conflict of interest between institutional productivity (free patient labour) and duty of care; prevalence rising anyway (syphilis? industrialization? diagnostic practice?). The answer adopted was degeneration.
Neurologists
1840s–1890s		The brain–behaviour link is confirmed in the 1860s, including frontal-lobe speech localization (Broca). By the 1870s the post-mortem brain examination is the main intervention. Kraepelin gives the first description of chronic psychotic disorders.By the 1890s anatomical study had reached its limit: results were inconsistent, normal brains turned up with pathology in life, cellular study was in its infancy — and demand for treatment was rising.
Psychoanalysis
1860s–1910s		Phenomenology leads to diagnosis. Freud, with Charcot at La Salpêtrière, shows hysterical paralysis differs from stroke paralysis (1893); with Breuer, Studies on Hysteria (1895). Treatment becomes possible.By 1897 all hysteria is traced to a forbidden childhood sexual fantasy. Psychoanalysis is codified by the 1910s — and then the First World War produces shell shock (Dr. Charles Myers), which the model cannot explain.
Somatic therapies
1930s		Anecdotal reports of brief lucidity after fevers or seizures. Five were tried: cold showers or baths; fever-inducing treatments; insulin-induced comas; electroconvulsive therapy; psychosurgery (lobotomies, cingulotomies, leucotomies).Research supporting all of these except ECT was consistently negative when done appropriately. Even ECT, developed to treat psychosis, was found most helpful for mood symptoms. Lobotomy became briefly extremely popular, with consent not rigorous and procedures done by various people, not only trained physicians.
Psychoanalysis, second wave
1940s–1970s		Wartime success at getting soldiers back into the war gives psychoanalysis preeminence, particularly in the US. Children orphaned by the wars become a source of study for "pathological behaviour".Amid backlash over changing gender roles, and misogyny, the "Bad Mother" is blamed for neuroticism and for outcomes as varied as homosexuality and communism. This is clearly untrue — but dismantling it took roughly 20 years of work by (mostly female) psychoanalysts and second-wave feminists.
Deinstitutionalization
1950s–1990s		Shell shock's best intervention had been community and responsibility to the platoon, treated on site with peers as mentors. 1964: Principles of Preventative Psychiatry, written after the Coconut Grove fire in Boston (492 deaths), moves care into local churches, schools and clinics. New drugs: chlorpromazine, imipramine, diazepam. Policy: the US 1955 Joint Commission on Mental Illness and Mental Health; in Canada, provincially organized bed closures.The main problems were four-fold: insufficient scale; inflexible, one-size-fits-all care; poor hospital–community integration; and stigma that excluded the most disruptive patients. The result was a surge in homelessness and repeat brief hospitalizations, and likely the surge of people with severe and persistent mental illness in carceral systems.

Degeneration — five false assumptions

  1. Evolution is a one-way process, guiding species, humans included, to their ideal version over time.
  2. Some humans are not suited to the biologic and cognitive stressors of modern life, owing to backwards or primitive traits.
  3. Individuals can devolve into a more primitive state, and these degenerating people can be identified by physical characteristics — shapes of ears, skull, face, "primitive races".
  4. Mental illness is due to this degeneration process.
  5. If so, there is no role for treatment — only observation and research, which is what produced the rise of the neurologists.

Assumption 5 is the hinge, and the clearest case of a social theory dictating clinical practice: because degeneration implied illness was inherited and irreversible, treatment was considered pointless and the discipline's energy went into post-mortem research instead.

Shell shock, and why the sexual-repression model collapsed

The explanation could not survive contact with male soldiers. Hysteria had been held to be a feminine disease, present in weak women with repressed sexual fantasies, so the idea that these symptoms came from repressed sexual fantasies was quickly thrown out. The symptoms were instead read as somehow connected to the experience of war, possibly "shocking" the nervous system. Menninger and colleagues treated them with talk therapy and hypnosis. The stated purpose is the part to remember: psychiatrists became crucial inside military systems in order to treat and return soldiers to the battlefield as soon as possible — the sharpest illustration in the module of social assumptions, not data, shaping diagnosis.

The rise of diagnostics

Social scientists raised four concerns: inter-rater reliability in diagnosis was very low — "as low as 30%" at times; Neo-Freudians held that diagnosis mattered less than the repressed ideas behind the symptoms; diagnosis was more often based on behaviour considered deviant than on symptoms causing suffering and impaired function; and there was a fundamental difference between intervening on objectively confirmable derangements of biology and on theoretical constructs. Three currents then converged.

  • St. Louis. By 1972 a group had built symptom-based checklists that could be assessed statistically for stability and validity, and refined until reliability was high enough.
  • Pharmaceutical companies needed an accurate, effective way to identify homogeneous enough groups of people — a genuine co-driver of operationalized diagnosis, not a footnote to it.
  • Homosexuality and the DSM. DSM-I was a compendium of mental illnesses used as a hospital resource to identify patients for census purposes, not treatment. DSM-II came out of the Second World War, was very Neo-Freudian, split "brain tissue diseases" from "psychogenic" diseases, and listed "diseases" that were behavioural deviances without clear dysfunction or distress. Dr. Evelyn Hooker, in the early 1950s, compared projective tests of 30 gay men and 30 age-matched controls and found no difference. At the 1972 American Psychiatric Association meeting, a gay psychiatrist addressed the assembly in a gas mask and wig, through a voice-distorting microphone, as Dr. H. Anonymous — John Fryer.
DSM-III — the three rules
1. For something to be considered a disorder, it must cause subjective distress and/or significant impairment in function. 2. Diagnosis is made not from expert opinion about the meaning of symptoms, but from a statistically validated checklist of signs and symptoms that can be reported by the patient or observed by the examiner. 3. A potential disorder is not included unless it can be reliably and stably identified by that process.

The module does not date DSM-III; the week's question key gives 1980 and treats DSM-III as the paradigm shift — DSM-I and DSM-II being narrative documents, and DSM-IV an update rather than a re-conceptualization.

Discriminators and exam traps

Mood vs affect — mood is what the patient says, affect is what you see, and affect takes three descriptors, not one.
Hallucination vs illusion — no stimulus vs a real stimulus misperceived.
MoCA vs MMSE — the MMSE is the better known but maybe less reliable one. Do not reverse them.
Insight vs judgment — insight is the three recognitions, judgment is acting on them, and both are required for capacity.
Egypt, not Greece, for the wandering uterus.
ECT — developed for psychosis, most helpful for mood.
Who did what — Myers described shell shock, Menninger treated it, Kraepelin gave the first description of chronic psychotic disorders, Hooker ran the 30-versus-30 study.
US vs Canada — a federal 1955 Joint Commission vs provincially organized bed closures.

The counts are examinable: four background forces, five degeneration assumptions, five somatic therapies, four deinstitutionalization failures, four social-scientist concerns, three DSM-III rules.

What is and is not on the exam. Dr. Byrne's own framing: you should look at the history module — "there might be a question from it", and it is not heavy going. The orientation reading is very general, with nothing to memorize. The introduction to nosology module is out: you do not need to open it, and there are no multiple-choice questions from it. Where he says you need not memorize something, he means you will be given clues rather than asked to regurgitate a slide — not that the concept is off the exam.

The module is one argument: psychiatry adopts a unifying explanation — humours, degeneration, neuroanatomy, psychoanalysis — over-applies it, and is corrected, until DSM-III replaced expert interpretation with a reliability-tested checklist that requires distress and/or impairment.

guides.title: Week 40 · 2 Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization
guides.html:
PW02 · NeuroPrimer · Neuro

Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The course's own dermatome, myotome and reflex standard, and the primer that turns it into a localization method: root vs cord, UMN vs LMN, and why the imaging you order depends on getting it right.

Definitions, and why the tables differ between books

  • Dermatome — the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres of a single spinal nerve, and therefore arising from a single spinal level.
  • Myotome — the group of muscle cells controlled by the somatic motor fibres of a single spinal nerve. Those cells may be distributed across several different muscles, so one myotome can control more than one movement.
  • Radiculopathy — a lesion of a nerve root. Myelopathy — a lesion of the spinal cord. Learn that pair verbatim; every localization answer in this week resolves to one or the other.

Anatomy textbooks and clinical textbooks give different root lists, the anatomy books typically being more inclusive. The clinical resolution is that most muscles are supplied predominantly by one root, or at most two, and it is that predominance that makes precise localization possible. The tables below are the ones used throughout this course, including assessments — they were built from clinical electromyography and neuromuscular texts plus consensus among several neuromuscular neurologists. Where another textbook disagrees, answer from these.

Localization is an intersection
Find the single root shared by every weak muscle. Biceps is predominantly C5 and C6; pronator teres is predominantly C6 and C7. Weakness in both therefore points to a single C6 lesion — (C5, C6) ∩ (C6, C7) = C6. Triceps is a predominantly C7 muscle, so triceps weakness with an intact biceps moves the lesion down a level. Do the intersection before you name a root.
Do not confuse a root lesion with a peripheral nerve lesion. Peripheral nerves form by overlapping of fibres within a plexus, so the cutaneous territory of one peripheral nerve spans portions of several dermatomes. The pad of the thumb is C6 and the pad of the middle finger is C7, yet both are reached by the same peripheral nerve, the median nerve. Numbness in thumb and middle finger together is a median nerve pattern; numbness confined to one of them is a root pattern.

Myotomes

Upper limb movementRoot(s)Lower limb movementRoot(s)
Abduction of shoulderC5Flexion of hipL2, L3
Flexion of elbowC5, C6Extension of hipS1
Extension of elbowC7Abduction and medial rotation of hipL5
Pronation of forearmC6, C7Adduction of hipL3, L4
Supination of forearmC6Extension of kneeL3, L4
Extension of wristC7Flexion of kneeL5, S1
Flexion of wristC7Dorsiflexion of ankleL5
Extension of digitsC7Plantarflexion of ankleS1
Flexion of digitsC8Inversion of ankleL5
Flexion of thumb at IP jointC8Eversion of ankleL5
Abduction and adduction of digitsC8, T1——

Two details of the table are worth fixing in memory. Wrist flexion and wrist extension are both C7, opposed movements sharing one root. And the course assigns both ankle inversion and ankle eversion to L5; many clinical texts split them into eversion L5–S1 and inversion L4–L5, but L5 for both is the course standard and the answer to give.

Dermatome test points

These are the points you actually touch when you screen a limb, one per level.

RootUpper limb test pointRootLower limb test point
C5Lateral upper armL1Groin / inguinal
C6ThumbL2Anterior mid-thigh
C7Middle fingerL3Medial knee
C8Little finger and medial border of the handL4Medial malleolus
T1Medial arm and medial forearmL5Dorsum of foot
——S1Lateral foot

The medial forearm band is T1, not C8 — C8 is the medial border of the hand running into the little finger. Posteriorly there is an axial line separating S2 from L5 and L4: a boundary where dermatomes that sit next to each other on the skin are not neighbouring spinal segments. Because the perineal dermatomes are concentric rings, saddle anaesthesia maps cleanly onto S2–S4, which is what makes it a discrete, testable red-flag finding rather than a vague complaint.

Root, movement, reflex and dermatome in one table

RootKey movement(s)ReflexDermatome
C5Shoulder abductionBiceps (C5, C6); brachioradialis (C5, C6)Lateral upper arm
C6Elbow flexion (C5, C6); supination; pronation (C6, C7)Biceps; brachioradialisThumb
C7Elbow extension, finger extension; wrist flexion and extensionTricepsMiddle finger
C8Finger flexion; thumb flexion at IP; finger abduction (C8, T1)—Little finger
T1Abduction and adduction of digits (C8, T1)—Medial arm
L1——Groin
L2Hip flexion (L2, L3)—Anterior mid-thigh
L3Hip flexion; hip adduction; knee extension (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial knee
L4Knee extension, hip adduction (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial malleolus
L5Ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction; eversion; knee flexion (L5, S1)—Dorsum of foot
S1Ankle plantarflexion, hip extension; knee flexion (L5, S1)AnkleLateral foot
S2–S4——Saddle / perineal

Note the empty reflex cells: there is no routinely tested reflex for C8, T1 or L5. An L5 radiculopathy therefore has to be caught on power and sensation — dorsiflexion, big toe extension, inversion, hip abduction, and the dorsum of the foot — because the reflexes will be normal.

The anatomy that drives localization

  • The cervical canal contains both the spinal cord and the exiting nerve roots, so a cervical disc can compress a nerve root (most common), the cord, or both, depending on its direction (central versus lateral) and size.
  • The spinal cord ends at L1. Below that the canal contains only the lumbosacral nerve roots, so a lumbar disc almost never affects the cord and involves roots alone.
  • Commonest degenerative levels: cervical C5–C6 and C6–C7, then C4–C5; lumbar L4–L5 and L5–S1, then L3–L4. These are also the levels whose radiculopathies you will see most often.
  • Keep the anatomy and the syndrome separate: the lumbosacral nerve roots are the structure; cauda equina syndrome is a clinical syndrome caused by compression of those roots.
Cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency
(a) Low back pain plus (b) saddle (perineal) anaesthesia plus (c) bladder and/or bowel dysfunction — urinary retention with overflow, or unrecognized faecal incontinence — with or without leg pain, sensory loss or weakness. It is a CORE Back Tool red flag. The same threshold applies above the conus: compressive myelopathy and cauda equina syndrome are both surgical emergencies once bladder and bowel function are compromised.

Radiculopathy on history is any one or more of: radicular pain, described as shooting or sharp and shock-like; numbness or tingling; weakness; and impaired bladder or bowel control. On examination a root lesion gives sensory loss in a dermatomal distribution and weakness in a myotomal distribution — which is the whole reason the two tables above have to be memorized.

Acute mechanism: the nucleus pulposus herniates. In the lumbar spine a lateral herniation impinges a single nerve root and produces a discrete radiculopathy; a central herniation can catch a whole group of roots and is the one that threatens cauda equina syndrome. Chronic mechanism: degenerative change narrows the canal and foramina over years — lumbar spinal stenosis. Three structures crowd the canal at once: thickened ligamentum flavum, hypertrophied facet joints, and a bulging disc. It presents as neurogenic claudication: pain, numbness and/or weakness and fatigue in the legs brought on by prolonged walking, worsened by extension of the back, and relieved by forward flexion or sitting down. That flexion-relief pattern is the discriminator from vascular claudication.

The neurological examination

ComponentWhat to do and what to look for
ToneRule out spasticity
BulkLook for atrophy in muscles sharing a myotome — triceps for C7, gastrocnemius for S1
Power, upper limbShoulder abduction (C5) · elbow flexion (C5, C6) · elbow extension and finger extension (C7) · finger flexion and abduction (C8)
Power, lower limbKnee extension and hip adduction (L3, L4) · ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction (L5) · ankle plantarflexion and hip extension (S1)
ReflexesBiceps (C5, C6) · brachioradialis (C5, C6) · triceps (C7) · knee (L3, L4) · ankle (S1) · rule out ankle clonus
Functional testsWalking on the heels for dorsiflexion · walking on the toes and single-leg toe raises for plantarflexion · tandem gait for balance
Plantar responseRule out an extensor response — the big toe extends, with or without fanning of the other toes: the Babinski sign
SensationReduced pinprick in a dermatomal distribution · rule out saddle anaesthesia (S2–S4) · rule out a sensory level
Provocative testsLumbar: straight leg raise (L4–S1) and femoral stretch test (L2–L4) · cervical: Spurling's test
A sensory level is not a dermatomal sensory loss. Dermatomal loss — one band, one level — means a root. A sensory level, a dermatomal level below which all sensation is lost, suggests a spinal cord lesion and changes both the urgency and the region you image. Test upward until you find where sensation becomes normal, and say which it is.

Worked example, S1 radiculopathy, one of the commonest radiculopathies you will meet: tone normal; atrophy of the gastrocnemius; weakness of ankle plantarflexion and hip extension; reduced or absent ankle reflex; flexor (normal) plantar response; reduced sensation over the lateral foot. Every element of that constellation is a lower motor neuron sign, and together they name both the level and the compartment.

Upper versus lower motor neuron

The motor pathway is a two-neuron chain spanning the CNS and the PNS. The upper motor neuron has its cell body in the primary motor cortex and descends to synapse on the lower motor neuron, whose cell body sits in the ventral horn and whose axon travels in a peripheral nerve to the neuromuscular junction. The CNS/PNS boundary falls between the lower motor neuron cell body and its axon, at the root exit — which is why a root lesion gives pure LMN signs.

ComponentUpper motor neuron lesionLower motor neuron lesion at a root
ToneIncreased — spasticityNormal or reduced
BulkNormalReduced — atrophy
PowerDiffuse, in an UMN pattern: extensors weaker than flexors in the upper limb, flexors weaker than extensors in the lower limbMyotomal
ReflexesIncreased, with ankle clonusReduced or absent, no clonus
Plantar responseExtensor — pathologicalFlexor — normal

Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in tone — a sudden resistance to quick passive movement of the limb, absent on slow movement. Ankle clonus is elicited with the hip and knee flexed together and the ankle quickly dorsiflexed. The primer introduced this table in the musculoskeletal block as background; it defers the detail to the Neuro block, and this is that block — know it by heart.

Leg weakness: lumbar spine or cervical spine?
Two things make the obvious answer unsafe. Back and neck pain often co-exist, and both a cervical cord lesion and a lumbar root lesion can produce lower limb symptoms alone. A cervical cord lesion strikes the UMN segment of the pathway to the leg; a lumbar root lesion strikes the LMN segment. So a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness — while a cervical nerve root lesion cannot. The discriminator is tone, reflexes and plantar response, and it is why the CORE Neck Tool asks about changes in walking and gait.

Why localization changes management

Localizing correctly is what lets you image the correct region. Get it wrong and you may be falsely reassured by a normal scan and miss the culprit. The worked error: a cervical disc compressing the cord causes progressive bilateral leg weakness and difficulty walking and needs urgent surgery; the examiner misses the UMN signs, assumes a lumbar cause, orders a lumbar MRI, and the pathology goes unfound — a delay that can end in permanent disability.

Why not simply image the whole spine? Three reasons. Resource stewardship. Time and tolerability — whole-spine imaging takes double to triple as long, and a claustrophobic patient who manages a single region in about 15–20 minutes will not manage close to an hour. And specificity — two-thirds of asymptomatic people show degenerative disc change on imaging, so an unlocalized scan generates findings you cannot interpret.

The closing discipline, for every back or neck pain patient, is three questions: (1) are there signs of a specific nerve root, and if so which one? (2) are there signs of the spinal cord rather than the roots? (3) are there signs of a surgical emergency — compressive myelopathy or cauda equina syndrome?

Discriminators and exam traps

  • C7 carries the most: elbow extension, wrist flexion and extension, digit extension, the triceps reflex, the middle finger. C8 is digit flexion and the little finger.
  • Elbow flexion is C5, C6 but supination is C6 alone; pronation is C6, C7.
  • Dorsiflexion L5, plantarflexion S1. Hip flexion L2, L3 but hip extension S1. Hip abduction L5 but hip adduction L3, L4.
  • Knee reflex L3–L4, ankle reflex S1, and nothing for C8, T1 or L5.
  • L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot — the three most often swapped.
  • Straight leg raise L4–S1, femoral stretch L2–L4, Spurling's for the cervical roots.
  • The cord ends at L1, so lumbar disc disease hits roots only, while cervical disc disease can hit root, cord or both.
  • In an LMN lesion tone is normal or reduced — normal tone does not exclude a radiculopathy, and the reflex and plantar findings carry the weight.
Localize before you image: take the single root shared by every weak muscle, then let tone, reflexes and the plantar response tell you root (LMN) or cord (UMN) — because a cervical cord lesion and a lumbar root lesion can look identical from the legs, and only one of them will appear on the scan you were about to order.

guides.title: Week 40 · 3 Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR
guides.html:
SLM02 · Neuroimaging

Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How CT and MR generate image contrast, what every sequence shows, and when to order which.

Attenuation: how x-rays make contrast

Imaging modalities divide by whether or not they use x-rays. X-ray based, with a radiation dose: plain films, cerebral angiography, myelography and CT. Not x-ray based: MRI. A heated cathode (−) produces electrons that accelerate to the anode (+) and strike a tungsten target — the x-rays arise at the target, not at the cathode.

The image depends entirely on attenuation: the degree to which x-rays are absorbed, which depends on the density of the material traversed. Learn the rule in this form:

  • High density → high attenuation → white on the image.
  • Low density → low attenuation → black on the image.

The reference materials, in order of decreasing density: lead → bone → muscle → water → fat → air. Every density question in this material — the quizzes, the Hounsfield table, the contrast agents — is that one ordering applied.

CT acquisition and Hounsfield units

CT is still x-ray attenuation, but sampled from many angles: a rotating x-ray source, rotating detectors and a moving table combine into a composite three-dimensional image. Hounsfield units (HU) convert those attenuation values into a visual greyscale, on a scale from −1000 to +1000.

MaterialHU rangeOn brain CT
Bone+400 to +10001000
Soft tissue+40 to +80muscle 60
Grey / white matter—80 / 50
Water, CSF00
Fat−60 to −100−100
Lung−400 to −600—
Air−1000−1000

The exact numbers do not need to be memorized, but the ordering does. Two consequences are heavily testable. First, grey matter (80 HU) is denser, and therefore brighter on CT, than white matter (50 HU) — the opposite of their relationship on T1. Second, ranked densest first: iodinated contrast > clotted blood > liquid blood > grey matter > white matter > CSF > fat. Clotted blood is denser than unclotted blood, which is exactly why acute hemorrhage looks hyperdense.

Windowing

Whiter pixels mean higher HU. A monitor cannot display the whole HU range at once, so the window/level settings select which slice of the range is spread across the available greys. Windowing changes nothing about the underlying data — the same acquisition viewed two ways looks like two different scans. Narrow window = high contrast, which amplifies the few-HU loss of grey–white differentiation in early stroke; wide window = lower contrast but a much wider range shown, giving headroom for dense blood alongside normal brain.

Two naming points are worth fixing before an exam. The prose in this module calls the centre point the "window" and the range the "level", which is the reverse of standard usage and of the module's own summary slide — conventionally W = window width = the range and L = level = the centre. And the brain window is printed twice with different numbers: once as a centre of 40 with a range of 100, and once as W80 L40; the centre of 40 agrees, the width does not, so expect either 80 or 100 for the width.

WindowSettingWhat it is for
BrainW80 L40routine parenchymal review
StrokeW30 L30subtle early ischemic hypodensity
BleedW200 L100hyperdense acute blood
Bonecentre 100, range 2000skull, trabecular detail, fractures

Blood on CT by age

Density falls as a clot ages and its protein breaks down, so the same collection changes colour over weeks:

  • Acute — hyperdense, roughly 50–70 HU, brighter than brain. This is the appearance the bleed window is designed to show.
  • Subacute — isodense with brain over days to a couple of weeks. This is the dangerous phase: a subdural collection can be nearly invisible, betrayed only by mass effect or a displaced grey–white junction.
  • Chronic — hypodense, approaching CSF density.

MR signal of blood by age is a separate, more complicated scheme and is not covered here; the working rule to carry is the blanket one — most pathology is bright on T2 and dark on T1 — plus GRE/SWI, where blood products are dark at every age.

Contrast, the blood–brain barrier and safety

All x-ray-based contrast, CT included, is iodine-based: high density → high attenuation → easily seen, and generally non-toxic. MR contrast is gadolinium, visible because it is bright on T1.

Iodinated (CT)Gadolinium (MR)
Why it is visiblehigh density → high attenuationbright on T1
Allergyyes — mild rash through to anaphylaxisyes, but rare
Renal harmcontrast-induced nephropathy; pre-existing renal insufficiency is the single most important risk factornephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure
Otherfluid overload—
Vessels without contrast?no — CTA and CTV both need IV contrastyes — time-of-flight for arteries, phase-contrast for veins

A contrast-enhanced CT head shows three things: cerebral arteries (CTA), cerebral veins (CTV), and regions of blood–brain barrier breakdown — tumour, infection, active inflammation. The mechanism is the single most examinable line here: the integrity of the vessel wall is compromised, so contrast leaks out of the intravascular space. Gadolinium enhancement on MR works by the identical mechanism, and adds the meninges, which is how meningitis enhances.

CTA versus CTV is purely a matter of timing — same injection, same scanner, early acquisition for arteries and late for veins. The MR-specific advantage is that vessels can be imaged with no contrast at all, at a quality described as similar to contrast-enhanced angiography or venography. In practice the non-contrast time-of-flight arterial images can be the crisper of the two; treat the two approaches as comparable rather than assuming contrast always wins.

Renal function matters for both agents, but the injuries are different and are commonly swapped. Iodinated contrast causes contrast-induced nephropathy — renal insufficiency is the risk factor, the kidney is the target. Gadolinium in established renal failure causes nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — renal failure is the risk factor, the skin and connective tissue are the target. Fluid overload is a third, separate iodinated-contrast effect. Screen for ferromagnetic implants and retained metallic foreign bodies before any MR: the static field can move or heat them.

The other x-ray-based modalities

  • Plain films — the best way to screen bone anatomy quickly, and give minimal information about the CNS.
  • Cerebral angiography — images intracranial vessels dynamically, but needs vascular access, usually a femoral puncture, and is therefore invasive; it also needs fluoroscopy and injected contrast.
  • Myelography — lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or lower, to stay below the conus, which ends at L1–L2. Contrast opacifies the CSF around the cord and cauda equina, so a mass or a stenosis appears as an indentation or a block in the white contrast column.

Invasive is the pivot word. CTA/CTV and MRA/MRV are the non-invasive counterparts of catheter angiography, and are the initial tests of choice for a suspected cerebral vascular abnormality.

How MR makes an image

The patient is placed in a strong magnetic field and spinning hydrogen protons align with it. A radiofrequency pulse tips that alignment away; when the pulse stops the protons relax back, releasing energy that is detected and reconstructed into an image. Two relaxation processes are measured, T1 and T2, and every tissue has its own characteristic T1 and T2 relaxation rates — that is the whole basis of MR contrast. The signal from a voxel, a three-dimensional volume of tissue, depends on the number of protons in it plus its T1 and T2. Images are produced by pulse sequences: gradients and RF pulses switched on and off in a choreographed pattern, each designed to interrogate a specific tissue attribute.

Ordering an MRI
A brain MRI automatically includes all of the standard sequences and you do not need to specify them — except MR angiogram and venogram, which must be requested by name. You must still write the diagnoses you want confirmed or ruled out on the requisition, because that is what determines the protocol.

The sequences and what each one shows

T1 versus T2: CSF is dark on T1 and bright on T2; white matter is whiter than grey on T1, and darker than grey on T2.

The one-second discriminator
Look at the CSF. Dark CSF = T1. Bright CSF = T2. Then apply the blanket rule: most pathology is bright on T2 and dark on T1.
  • FLAIR — T2-weighted, but with the CSF signal suppressed. It is the sequence for edema and demyelination, because a T2-bright lesion sitting next to a T2-bright ventricle is camouflaged until the CSF is turned off. Periventricular MS plaques are the classic demonstration: invisible-ish on plain T2, conspicuous on FLAIR.
  • DWI with ADC — DWI measures the random Brownian motion of water; the apparent diffusion coefficient, in mm²/s, quantifies it. Low ADC means restricted diffusion, which appears bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map. The two are always acquired and read together, because T2 signal alone can make a lesion look bright on DWI. Causes of restricted diffusion, in order of frequency: acute ischemia or stroke, most commonly, through cellular swelling; densely cellular tumours, typically malignant; and abscess. The stroke mechanism is worth stating precisely — cell death produces cytotoxic edema, water accumulates inside cells, and free movement of water between intracellular and extracellular space is restricted.
  • GRE / SWI — identifies hemorrhage and calcification, both of which appear dark, because both distort the local field: blood products are paramagnetic, calcium and bone are diamagnetic. Multiple small round black dots scattered through the cortex of an older patient are the microhemorrhages of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, a cause of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage.
  • T1 with gadolinium — shows where the blood–brain barrier has broken down. Two enhancement patterns can coexist in a single lesion: a blush (diffuse, hazy) and a ring (bright rim around a non-enhancing centre).
  • MRA / MRV — arteries and veins, obtainable without contrast, and the only sequences that must be requested by name.

Signal cheat sheet

Tissue or findingCTT1 / T2FLAIR · DWI-ADC · GRE
CSF / water0 HU, darkdark / brightFLAIR dark (suppressed); ADC bright
Grey matter80 HU, brighter than whiterelatively dark / relatively brightFLAIR keeps T2-type contrast
White matter50 HU, darker than greyrelatively bright / relatively dark—
Bone / air / fat+400 to +1000 / −1000 / −60 to −100air black; fat bright on T1GRE: bone dark, diamagnetic
Iodinated contrast / gadoliniumdensest thing on the scalegadolinium bright on T1—
Acute blood, clottedhyperdense, denser than liquid blood; bleed windowbright on T2, dark on T1 as a first approximationGRE dark (paramagnetic)
Chronic microhemorrhageoften invisible—GRE: black dots — amyloid angiopathy
Edemahypodensedark / brightFLAIR bright
Demyelination—dark / bright, but camouflaged next to CSFFLAIR bright and conspicuous
Acute infarctsubtle hypodensity; stroke window—DWI bright / ADC dark
Malignant tumour / abscessenhances — barrier broken; ring enhancementblush and/or ring after gadoliniumcan restrict diffusion
Calcificationdense, bright—GRE dark (diamagnetic)

CT versus MR: when to order which

AxisCTMR
Basis and radiationx-ray attenuation and density, in Hounsfield units, viewed through a chosen window; iodine contrast; radiation doseproton relaxation (T1, T2) and proton number per voxel, via pulse sequences; gadolinium; no radiation
Availabilityfar more available, much easier to obtain urgently in the EDslower and scarcer; typically the planned or outpatient study
Subtle abnormalitylower sensitivityhigher sensitivity
Typical usesbone pathology — fractures, dislocations, metastases; acute hemorrhage; trauma; acute strokebrain parenchymal pathology, using sequence-specific information
Urgent vessel questionpreferred — CTA or CTV, e.g. large-vessel occlusion in acute strokenot preferred when the answer is needed now
Contrast allergy or pregnancyavoidpreferred — and can be done with no contrast at all
Ordering mechanicsspecify contrast and phaseall sequences automatic except MRA and MRV
The four deciders
For most vascular questions the information from CT and MR is comparable, so diagnostic yield is rarely what decides. What decides: urgency and availability → CT; already getting an MRI, or needing higher sensitivity for a subtle lesion → MR; prior iodinated-contrast allergy → MR; pregnancy or any reason to avoid radiation → MR.

The module's own questions, worked

Lateral skull film, two arrows on the cranial vault — is attenuation high or low? Keyed high. Both arrows sit on skull bone: high density → high attenuation → white. Low is wrong because low attenuation appears black, and the arrowed regions are white.

Lateral cervical spine, one arrow on the dark band anterior to the vertebral bodies — keyed low. The arrow is on the air-filled airway: low density → low attenuation → black. The pair test a single skill — map the greyscale value under the arrow back onto the density ladder.

Worked case: a 36-year-old man presents to the ER after a seizure, and a CT is shown before and after contrast, each asked "is this normal?" Non-contrast: no — there is subtle hyperdensity in the right occipital lobe, which you would not be expected to detect at this stage of training. Post-contrast: no, and the abnormality is no longer subtle once intravenous contrast is given — it is a right occipital arteriovenous malformation. The expectation is that you recognize the study is abnormal and that contrast unmasked the lesion, not that you make the specific diagnosis from the images alone.

DWI/ADC self-test. Two panels are shown with three questions — which is the DWI and which the ADC, where is the restricted diffusion, and what is the differential. There is no keyed answer available for this one, so do not treat any specific diagnosis as the intended answer. Reason it out instead: the panel with dark CSF and bright parenchyma is the DWI and the one with bright CSF is the ADC map; restricted diffusion is the area that is bright on DWI and dark on ADC; and the defensible differential is the standard three — acute ischemia or stroke, densely cellular malignant tumour, abscess.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Grey/white brightness flips between modalities — grey matter is brighter on CT, white matter is brighter on T1. Getting this backwards misreads both.
  • Clotted blood is denser than liquid blood, which is why acute hemorrhage is bright on CT and why a subacute collection fades to isodense.
  • Enhancement is leakage, not uptake. Contrast appears where the vessel wall has lost integrity, not where a tissue has taken the agent up.
  • GRE does not distinguish hemorrhage from calcification — both are dark; only the adjective (paramagnetic versus diamagnetic) differs. Correlate with CT, where calcium is bright and old blood often is not.
  • MR can image vessels with no contrast at all; CT cannot. CTA and CTV always require an injection.
  • Window settings change the picture, never the data — a "negative" CT read on the wrong window is not a negative CT.
Dark CSF is not uniquely T1. FLAIR also shows dark CSF, but keeps T2-type parenchymal contrast, so a lesion that is bright on FLAIR next to dark CSF is not a T1-bright lesion. Check whether the periventricular white matter carries T2-type contrast before you call a sequence T1.
Density decides CT — high density → high attenuation → white, measured in Hounsfield units and displayed through a chosen window; proton relaxation decides MR — dark CSF = T1, bright CSF = T2, FLAIR = T2 with CSF suppressed, DWI bright with ADC dark = restricted diffusion, GRE dark = blood or calcium, gadolinium bright on T1; and on either modality, enhancement means contrast has leaked through a broken blood–brain barrier.

guides.html:
SLM06 · Embryology

Development of the Brain

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Neurulation, neural tube defects, the five vesicles and their cavities, and how grey matter ends up on the outside.

Where the nervous system comes from

The CNS has a single embryological source — the neural tube. The PNS has two — the neural tube and the neural crest. The brain is part of the CNS, so the whole story of brain development begins with the tube.

The neural tube is built twice

The neural tube forms from two separate tissue sources, by two distinctly different morphogenetic mechanisms. In primary neurulation the tube forms by folding of ectoderm. In secondary neurulation it forms by condensation and cavitation of mesoderm left over from the primitive streak. The two lumens then join, and the result is one continuous cavity.

Primary neurulationSecondary neurulation
SourceEctoderm, induced over the notochordMesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak
Mechanismfolding: plate → folds → groove → fusion → tube, then delaminationcondensation into a solid medullary cord, cavitation, and mesenchymal-to-epithelial transformation
Productprimary neural tube — brain and most of the spinal cordsecondary neural tube — the most caudal spinal cord
Timingclosure complete in the 4th week; rostral neuropore ~25 days, caudal ~28 daysafter the caudal neuropore has closed

Ectoderm versus mesoderm is the cleanest discriminator, and the sequencing rule — secondary neurulation only begins once the caudal neuropore is shut — is the second.

Primary neurulation, step by step

Induction occurs in the ectoderm overlying the notochord and is organized by the notochord. It converts that ectoderm into neuroectoderm, forming the neural plate — a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, also called the neuroepithelium. The switch is visible at the molecular level: surface (epidermal) ectoderm expresses L-CAM and E-cadherin, while induced neuroectoderm switches to N-CAM and N-cadherin.

Three named stages follow:

  1. Elevation of the neural folds. The edges of the neural plate lift, bordering a midline neural groove.
  2. Apposition, contact and fusion. The folds move together, touch, and fuse across the midline to form the neural tube.
  3. Delamination. The tube separates from the overlying surface ectoderm.

At about 22 days the dorsal view shows somites flanking the groove and neural crest arising at the crest of the folds, going on to become the dorsal root ganglion.

Why delamination matters
Separation of the tube from the surface does two things at once. It lets the surface ectoderm fuse across the midline, giving the skin over the CNS. And it opens a space for mesoderm to migrate in between tube and ectoderm, giving the bone and the other connective-tissue coverings. The coverings of the CNS exist because the tube let go of the surface.

Closure timing. Closure begins at what will become the cervical spinal cord and proceeds rostrally and caudally at the same time, finishing in the 4th week — often before the pregnancy is recognized. The last two points to close are the rostral and caudal neuropores: the rostral at about 25 days after fertilization, the caudal at about 28 days. Those day numbers are the hard timing data worth memorizing.

Secondary neurulation

The remnant of the primitive streak lies just caudal to the caudal neuropore. Once that neuropore has closed, this mesoderm condenses into a rod-like medullary cord. Its cells lose their unpolarized, stellate mesenchymal appearance and take on a polarized epithelial one — mesenchymal-to-epithelial transformation — becoming a pseudostratified columnar neuroepithelium arranged radially around a cavity. That secondary cavity then becomes continuous with the lumen of the primary neural tube, completing neural tube development.

The slides and the narration order the two middle steps differently — the slides put the epithelial transformation before the cavity appears, the narration has the lumen develop first and the surrounding cells transform around it. The end state is identical, so either order is defensible; know both steps and do not be thrown if the sequence is asked.

Open neural tube defects

When the neural folds fail to come together, the result is an open neural tube defect. These defects cluster around the rostral and caudal neuropores, for a simple mechanical reason: the neuropores are the last regions to close, so they have the longest window in which to fail.

  • Incidence 1 in 1000 pregnancies.
  • Risk factors: family history, diabetes mellitus, obesity, anticonvulsant use.
  • Most cases have unknown etiology.
  • Folic acid supplementation reduces risk.
Neuropore that failsShould closeResulting defectRegion
Rostral (anterior)~25 daysAnencephalycranial — brain and vault; incompatible with life
Caudal (posterior)~28 daysMyeloschisisspinal cord — an open mid- to lower-back lesion
Anencephaly is not a failure of the brain to form. The brain tissue does form. Because the rostral neuropore stays open, the neural plate remains exposed to amniotic fluid and the tissue progressively deteriorates. It is destruction of tissue that was made, not absence of tissue that was never made — the commonest way this is asked, and the commonest way it is answered wrongly.

Note how the folate point and the timing point fit together. Closure is finished by about 28 days, which for most patients is before a pregnancy is even suspected. That is why folic acid has to be in place before and around conception to do anything — a supplement started at the first antenatal visit is already too late for neurulation. The module states that folic acid supplementation reduces risk and stops there, without specifying a dose.

Flexures

Once the tube has closed, its rostral end undergoes a series of bends and dilatations. The bends are flexures; the dilatations are vesicles. Three flexures are named:

  • Cervical flexure — where the future spinal cord meets the future brain; a ventral bend.
  • Cephalic (mesencephalic) flexure — at the future midbrain; also a ventral bend.
  • Pontine flexure — in the region of the developing pons, a very acute, sharp bend.

Only the pontine flexure is given a histogenetic consequence, and it is a big one: it everts the alar plates, rearranging the sensory and motor columns of the brainstem. Come back to this under the alar and basal plates below.

Vesicles, derivatives and cavities

The rostral dilatations first form three primary vesicles — prosencephalon, mesencephalon and rhombencephalon — which then subdivide into five secondary vesicles: the prosencephalon into telencephalon and diencephalon, the mesencephalon staying as it is, and the rhombencephalon into metencephalon and myelencephalon. Those five, plus the rest of the tube, give the whole adult CNS and the whole ventricular system.

VesicleAdult derivativeCavity
TelencephalonCerebral hemisphereLateral ventricles
DiencephalonDiencephalonThird ventricle
MesencephalonMidbrainCerebral aqueduct
MetencephalonPons and cerebellumFourth ventricle
MyelencephalonMedullaFourth ventricle
Rest of the neural tubeSpinal cordCentral canal
Three "only" facts in that table
The diencephalon is the only vesicle whose name does not change on the way to the adult. The metencephalon is the only vesicle with two derivatives (pons and cerebellum). The fourth ventricle is the only cavity supplied by two vesicles (metencephalon and myelencephalon). And the table's real message, in one line: the ventricular system is simply the lumen of the neural tube, regionally dilated.

Expansion of the hemispheres. Fetal brains at 5, 6, 7 and 8 months and at term show a surface that is essentially smooth until about the 5th to 6th month, gyrifying through the last trimester. The mechanism is mechanical: the telencephalic vesicles grow back over most of the other vesicles, then keep expanding while constrained by the developing skull, so the surface folds. The insula folds in first, then the rest of the gyri and sulci appear. The optic vesicle buds from the diencephalon early, but the eye is not followed further here.

Histogenesis: the three zones of the tube wall

Cells born at the lumen migrate outward, and the wall sorts itself into three concentric zones. This is the single scheme that explains grey and white matter.

ZonePositionCells and fateAdult identity
Ventricularinnermost, against the lumenproliferating neuroectoderm that stays putEpendyma
Intermediate (mantle)middleneuroblasts → neurons, glioblasts → glia; neuroblast cell bodies stop hereGrey matter
Marginaloutermostaxons extended outward from those neuroblasts; glioblasts follow and become oligodendrogliaWhite matter

The marginal zone starts as a layer of bare axons. It becomes white matter because some glioblasts migrate out into it, differentiate into oligodendroglia, and myelinate those fibres. Myelin is what converts the marginal zone into white matter.

Alar and basal plates

Within the intermediate zone, neuroblasts accumulate in two columns. Dorsal accumulation creates the alar plates, whose neurons become interneurons receiving input from the fibres of primary sensory neurons in the periphery. Ventral accumulation creates the basal plates, giving motor neurons that grow their axons out into the periphery — both somatic motor and preganglionic autonomic.

Alar plateBasal plate
Position in the spinal cordDorsal; midline partner the roof plateVentral; midline partner the floor plate
Neurons producedInterneurons receiving primary sensory inputMotor — somatic and preganglionic autonomic
At the fourth ventricle, after eversionLateralMedial
Boundary between themSulcus limitansSulcus limitans

At the level of the fourth ventricle — that is, the metencephalon and myelencephalon — the pontine flexure everts the alar plates, swinging them laterally as the roof plate is stretched thin. So the arrangement flips from sensory dorsal, motor ventral in the spinal cord to sensory lateral, motor medial in the floor of the fourth ventricle, with the sulcus limitans still marking the boundary in both.

The alar plate does not contain the sensory neuron. The primary sensory neuron cell body sits in the spinal ganglion and is neural-crest-derived, outside the cord entirely. What the alar plate holds is the interneuron that receives that fibre's input. Saying "the alar plate becomes the sensory neurons" is the classic error.
Alar plate, displaced laterally
Three brainstem nuclei are worth naming as alar-plate derivatives forced laterally by the pontine flexure: the vestibular nucleus, the spinal nucleus of CN V, and the solitary nucleus. All three are sensory, and all three sit lateral precisely because of the eversion.

The cerebellum

The cerebellum develops at the dorsal edges of the metencephalon — at the rhombic lip, the dorsolateral tip of the everted alar column — and grows to cover the fourth ventricle. The two hemispheres begin dorsally, merge with each other in the midline, and enlarge until the cerebellum roofs the ventricle it grew beside. The same alar column also sends cells migrating ventrally to form the pontine nuclei and the olivary nucleus.

Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus

The Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation often accompanies open neural tube defects of the spinal cord. The chain is mechanical and worth reciting in order:

  1. An open spinal NTD tethers the cord and pulls the hindbrain down.
  2. Parts of the cerebellum and medulla are displaced inferiorly into the foramen magnum.
  3. The displaced cerebellum compresses the foramen of Magendie — the median aperture of the fourth ventricle — against the medulla.
  4. CSF produced in the ventricles cannot escape into the subarachnoid space.
  5. It accumulates within the ventricles → hydrocephalus.
  6. Relief is a shunt placed into the ventricles and tunneled under the skin into a body cavity, usually draining to the abdomen, in some cases to the heart.

Hydrocephalus itself is taken up in week 41; what this module owns is the embryological chain from spinal defect to blocked outflow.

Radial glia and the migration disorders

The three-zone plan puts grey matter inside and white matter outside — exactly what the spinal cord looks like. But the cerebral and cerebellar cortices are grey and outermost, the reverse. So how does grey matter get to the outside?

The answer is radial glial cells, which conduct migrating neuroblasts out to the cortex in both cerebrum and cerebellum. A radial glial cell spans the full width of the tube wall, from the ventricular surface all the way to the marginal zone. Neurons born in the ventricular zone climb along it until they can go no further, and settle there — which is why the cortex builds up from the inside out. In the cortical wall the three basic zones are refined to five: from the ventricle outward, ventricular → subventricular → intermediate → cortical plate → marginal.

When that migration fails, the grey matter stops short, and the clinical presentation is epilepsy and developmental delay.

DisorderWhat the MRI showsGene
Subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex")bands of grey matter interposed in the white matter between the cortex and the lateral ventriclesDCX
Periventricular nodular heterotopiagrey matter fails to migrate and remains along the lateral ventriclesFLNA

The position of the ectopic grey matter tells you how far the migration got. Grey still lining the ventricle means migration never really started — periventricular nodular heterotopia, FLNA. Grey stranded part-way out means migration arrested in transit — subcortical band heterotopia, DCX. Both are recognized on the grey/white signal pattern, not on the gyral pattern.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • CNS = neural tube only; PNS = neural tube + neural crest.
  • Primary = ectoderm by folding; secondary = primitive-streak mesoderm by condensation and cavitation, and secondary begins only after the caudal neuropore closes.
  • Rostral neuropore ~25 days → anencephaly; caudal ~28 days → myeloschisis — both within week 4, at the last regions to close.
  • Anencephaly is degeneration of tissue that did form after exposure to amniotic fluid, not failure to form.
  • Ventricular → ependyma, intermediate → grey, marginal → white; myelination by oligodendroglia is what makes the marginal zone white.
  • Sensory dorsal / motor ventral in the cord becomes sensory lateral / motor medial at the fourth ventricle, sulcus limitans the boundary at both levels, pontine flexure the cause.
  • Grey is inside in the cord but outside in the cortex — radial glia are the whole reason, and their failure is the heterotopias.
The neural tube is built twice — ectoderm by folding, primitive-streak mesoderm by condensation and cavitation — yet ends as one lumen. Its rostral dilatations become the five vesicles whose cavities are the ventricular system, and its wall is three zones: ventricular to ependyma, intermediate to grey, marginal to white. Every clinical item follows from that plan — the neuropores close last so defects cluster there, the pontine flexure everts alar into lateral, and radial glia are what carry grey matter to the outside.
