SLM07 · PD Module 1

Personality Disorders: Definitions, General Criteria & the Ten PDs

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What separates a personality trait from a personality disorder, the general criteria A–F that apply to all ten PDs, the three clusters, and the criteria and threshold for every PD except borderline.

Trait vs disorder

TermDefinition
Personality traitAn enduring pattern of perceiving and relating to the environment that is exhibited across a wide range of contexts
Personality disorderPresent when a person's personality traits cause them distress or impair their functioning

The trait itself is never the diagnosis. The step from trait to disorder is distress or functional impairment — nothing else. And having a personality disorder does not mean someone has a "bad personality": a person with one can still be kind, entertaining, charismatic, passionate and engaging.

General diagnostic criteria A–F

These apply to every personality disorder. A patient must meet all six before you count the disorder-specific criteria.

Criterion
AAn enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual's culture, manifested in ≥2 of these four areas: 1. Cognition — ways of perceiving and interpreting self, other people and events; 2. Affectivity — range, intensity, lability and appropriateness of emotional response; 3. Interpersonal functioning; 4. Impulse control
BThe pattern is inflexible and pervasive across a broad range of personal and social situations
CIt leads to clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning
DIt is stable and of long duration, with onset traceable to at least adolescence or early adulthood
ENot better explained as a manifestation or consequence of another mental disorder
FNot attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (drug of abuse, medication) or another medical condition such as head trauma
Memory hook for criterion A
The four domains are "CAIr": Cognition, Affect, Interpersonal, impulse Regulation. You need 2 of 4 — not all four, and not just one.
Traps on the general criteria
→ A pattern that began after a head injury, or only while using a substance, fails E/F — not a personality disorder.
→ A pattern confined to one setting, only at work say, fails pervasiveness (B).
→ Recent onset in mid-adulthood with no earlier history fails D.
→ A personality disorder can be diagnosed under age 18 if the traits are pervasive, persistent for ≥1 year and not limited to a developmental stage — except antisocial personality disorder, which requires age ≥18.

Etiology and management in general

  • Etiology, all personality disorders: an interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental influences — not primarily environmental.
  • No medication is approved to treat a personality disorder directly. Drugs are used for comorbidities or specific symptoms only.
  • Psychotherapy is the mainstay of management for most personality disorders.

The three clusters

ClusterOne wordCharacterDisorders
AEccentric (odd)PhoebeParanoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal
BIntense (dramatic)RachelAntisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic
CAnxiousMonicaAvoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-compulsive

Count check: A = 3, B = 4, C = 3 → ten disorders. The module deliberately discourages "mad, bad and sad" as a cluster mnemonic — it calls it somewhat derogatory and not particularly accurate. Use eccentric, intense, anxious instead, and learn the character-to-cluster pairing, which is how the module itself cues the three groups.

Cluster A — Eccentric

Key idea: Cluster A criteria resemble features of schizophrenia but are similar to, not the same as schizophrenia — no true hallucinations or delusions. Schizotypal resembles the positive symptoms (odd beliefs, perceptual distortions, odd speech); schizoid the negative symptoms (detachment, flat affect, anhedonia, asociality); paranoid resembles paranoid delusions (suspicion, mistrust) without reaching them. For all three, the pattern must not occur exclusively during schizophrenia, a bipolar or depressive disorder with psychotic features, or another psychotic disorder — and for schizoid and schizotypal, not exclusively during autism spectrum disorder.

Schizotypal — 5 of 9

Acute discomfort in close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, and eccentricities of behaviour.

  1. Ideas of reference, excluding delusions of reference
  2. Odd beliefs or magical thinking inconsistent with subcultural norms — superstitiousness, clairvoyance, telepathy, a "sixth sense"
  3. Unusual perceptual experiences, including bodily illusions
  4. Odd thinking and speech — vague, circumstantial, metaphorical, overelaborate, stereotyped
  5. Suspiciousness or paranoid ideation
  6. Inappropriate or constricted affect
  7. Behaviour or appearance that is odd, eccentric or peculiar
  8. Lack of close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives
  9. Excessive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity, tied to paranoid fears rather than negative self-judgement

Schizoid — 4 of 7

Detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotional expression.

  1. Neither desires nor enjoys close relationships, including being part of a family
  2. Almost always chooses solitary activities
  3. Little, if any, interest in sexual experiences with another person
  4. Takes pleasure in few, if any, activities
  5. Lacks close friends or confidants other than first-degree relatives
  6. Appears indifferent to praise or criticism of others
  7. Emotional coldness, detachment or flattened affectivity

Paranoid — 4 of 7

Distrust and suspiciousness such that others' motives are interpreted as malevolent.

  1. Suspects, without sufficient basis, that others are exploiting, harming or deceiving them
  2. Preoccupied with unjustified doubts about the loyalty or trustworthiness of friends
  3. Reluctant to confide in others, for unwarranted fear the information will be used maliciously
  4. Reads hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks or events
  5. Persistently bears grudges
  6. Perceives attacks on character or reputation not apparent to others; quick to react angrily or counterattack
  7. Recurrent unjustified suspicions about a partner's fidelity

Cluster B — Intense

Borderline personality disorder is covered in its own later modules. Its core pattern is instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, together with marked impulsivity, and its threshold is 5 of 9.

Narcissistic — 5 of 9

Grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy.

  1. Grandiose sense of self-importance — expects recognition as superior without commensurate achievement
  2. Preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty or ideal love
  3. Believes they are special and unique, understandable only by other special or high-status people
  4. Requires excessive admiration
  5. Sense of entitlement
  6. Interpersonally exploitative
  7. Lacks empathy — unwilling to recognize others' feelings and needs
  8. Often envious of others, or believes others are envious of them
  9. Arrogant, haughty behaviours or attitudes

Antisocial — 3 of 7, plus age and conduct-disorder requirements

Disregard for, and violation of, the rights of others.

  1. Failure to conform to social norms regarding lawful behaviour — repeated acts that are grounds for arrest
  2. Deceitfulness — repeated lying, aliases, conning for personal profit or pleasure
  3. Impulsivity or failure to plan ahead
  4. Irritability and aggressiveness — repeated physical fights or assaults
  5. Reckless disregard for safety of self or others
  6. Consistent irresponsibility — failure to sustain work or honour financial obligations
  7. Lack of remorse

Mandatory in addition: at least 18 years old, and evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15.

Psychopathy is not a DSM diagnosis
It is identified with the Hare Psychopathy Checklist–Revised (PCL-R). Most people with psychopathy probably also meet criteria for antisocial personality disorder, but many people with antisocial personality disorder do not have psychopathy.

Histrionic — 5 of 8

Excessive emotionality and attention seeking.

  1. Uncomfortable when not the centre of attention
  2. Inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behaviour
  3. Rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions
  4. Consistently uses physical appearance to draw attention to self
  5. Speech excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail
  6. Self-dramatization, theatricality, exaggerated emotional expression
  7. Suggestible
  8. Considers relationships more intimate than they actually are

Cluster C — Anxious

Obsessive-compulsive — 4 of 8

Preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control.

  1. Preoccupied with details, rules, lists, order or schedules to the extent that the major point of the activity is lost
  2. Perfectionism that interferes with task completion
  3. Excessively devoted to work to the exclusion of leisure and friendships, not explained by economic necessity
  4. Overconscientious, inflexible about morality, ethics or values, not explained by culture or religion
  5. Unable to discard worn-out or worthless objects
  6. Reluctant to delegate unless others submit to exactly their way
  7. Miserly spending style; money hoarded for future catastrophes
  8. Rigidity and stubbornness

Against OCD: obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is a pervasive personality style, usually ego-syntonic — the patient sees it as the right way to live — with no true obsessions or compulsions. OCD is discrete, usually ego-dystonic, and has them.

Avoidant — 4 of 7

Social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation.

  1. Avoids occupational activities with significant interpersonal contact, fearing criticism or rejection
  2. Unwilling to get involved with people unless certain of being liked
  3. Restraint within intimate relationships, fearing shame or ridicule
  4. Preoccupied with being criticized or rejected in social situations
  5. Inhibited in new interpersonal situations because of feelings of inadequacy
  6. Views self as socially inept, personally unappealing or inferior
  7. Unusually reluctant to take personal risks or try new activities that may prove embarrassing

Dependent — 5 of 8

Excessive need to be reassured and taken care of.

  1. Difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice and reassurance
  2. Needs others to assume responsibility for most major areas of life
  3. Difficulty expressing disagreement for fear of losing support — do not count realistic fears of retribution
  4. Difficulty initiating projects on their own, from lack of self-confidence, not lack of motivation or energy
  5. Goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance, even volunteering for unpleasant things
  6. Uncomfortable or helpless when alone, fearing being unable to care for self
  7. Urgently seeks another relationship when a close one ends
  8. Unrealistically preoccupied with fears of being left to take care of self

Threshold cheat sheet

DisorderThresholdSpecial requirements
Paranoid4/7—
Schizoid4/7—
Schizotypal5/9—
Antisocial3/7Age ≥18 and conduct disorder before 15
Borderline5/9Criteria covered in the later borderline modules
Histrionic5/8—
Narcissistic5/9—
Avoidant4/7—
Dependent5/8Do not count realistic fear of retribution in criterion 3
Obsessive-compulsive4/8Work devotion not due to economic necessity; morality not due to culture or religion
Pattern to remember
The three 4/7s are paranoid, schizoid, avoidant. The 5/9s are schizotypal, narcissistic, borderline. The 5/8s are histrionic, dependent. Obsessive-compulsive is 4/8. Antisocial is 3/7 — the lowest bar of the ten, and the only one with an age floor.

Discriminators and look-alikes

PresentationThinkNotWhy
Loner, flat affect, does not want friendsSchizoidAvoidantNo desire for relationships at all
Wants friends but avoids them for fear of rejectionAvoidantSchizoidDesire present; fear of criticism
Magical thinking, odd speech, ideas of reference, no fixed delusionsSchizotypalSchizophreniaNo true hallucinations or delusions
Suspicious, bears grudges, sees insults in benign remarks, no fixed delusionsParanoidDelusional disorderPervasive trait, not psychotic
Social anxiety persisting with familiarity, paranoid in flavourSchizotypalAvoidantParanoid fears, not negative self-judgement
Seeks admiration, entitled, no empathyNarcissisticHistrionicAdmiration and superiority, not attention and emotionality
Rigid perfectionist who never finishes tasks, will not delegateObsessive-compulsiveOCDPersonality pattern, no true obsessions or compulsions
Cannot decide anything without reassurance; cannot be aloneDependentAvoidantFear of being uncared for, not fear of rejection
16-year-old with repeated theft, fights and lyingConduct disorderAntisocialAntisocial requires age ≥18
The two discriminators the module states outright
→ Why do they want attention? Histrionic wants attention itself, with shallow emotions. Narcissistic wants admiration that confirms superiority, and lacks empathy. Borderline shows instability plus impulsivity with fear of abandonment.
→ Dependent criterion 4: poor initiation from low confidence points to dependent; poor initiation from low energy or motivation points to depression.

Worked examples

The module's own practice vignettes, with its answers:

  • Solitary software tester, indifferent to praise or criticism → schizoid. Avoidant patients want relationships, and there are no odd beliefs, so not schizotypal.
  • Talks about energy fields, speaks in metaphors, still uneasy at a book club after two years → schizotypal.
  • 19-year-old with three arrests → the missing requirement is conduct disorder before age 15.
  • Accountant who redoes spreadsheets, will not delegate, hoards broken electronics and sees nothing wrong with any of it → obsessive-compulsive.
  • Suspiciousness beginning six months after a traumatic brain injury → fails criterion F, and D as well.
  • Cannot order at a restaurant without her partner, moved in with a new partner within a week of a breakup → dependent, Cluster C.
  • Flirtatious, shifting emotions, calls a new acquaintance her best friend, gives no detail about a "terrible" week → histrionic.
  • Asked for management → psychotherapy is the mainstay; medications target comorbidities or specific symptoms; etiology is a gene–environment interaction, not primarily environmental.
Ten disorders, three clusters, one set of general criteria: an enduring, inflexible, pervasive pattern in ≥2 of 4 domains causing distress or impairment, present since adolescence or early adulthood, not explained by another disorder, a substance or a medical condition. Only then count the disorder-specific criteria against its own threshold — antisocial 3/7 is the lowest, and the only one with an age floor.

guides.title: Week 40 · 6 Borderline Personality Disorder: Etiology and Criteria
guides.html:
SLM08–09 · PD Modules 2–3

Borderline Personality Disorder: Etiology and Criteria

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why BPD earns four modules, the biosocial theory of an emotionally sensitive temperament meeting an invalidating environment, and the nine DSM criteria with the 5-of-9 threshold, worked through Victoria's case.

Why BPD matters: common, serious, treatable

SettingPrevalence of BPD
General population2–6%
Primary care6%
Psychiatry outpatient clinics10%
Psychiatric inpatients20%

There is no sex difference in community samples. The ladder runs 2–6 → 6 → 10 → 20.

  • Health-care use: people who self-harm use emergency services more than people with other chronic conditions — 232 ED visits per 100 person-years against 117.6 for asthma, plus more phone calls, prescriptions and referrals than other personality disorders.
  • Suicide: an 8–10% lifetime rate of completed suicide, comparable to schizophrenia and depression.
  • Self-harm: in about three quarters of patients — cutting, burning, overdosing.
  • Treatable: 75% improve with Dialectical Behaviour Therapy.

The biosocial model

BPD is a transaction: a child born with an emotionally sensitive temperament (the biological half) growing up in an invalidating environment (the social half). Neither half is the disorder on its own — the repeated interaction between them, over years, produces it.

BiologicalSocial
Emotionally intense temperament, with a family history of the sameInvalidating environment
Inherited trait of impulsivityTrauma
Bullying
Maternal separation

Biological: the emotionally sensitive temperament

Emotional reactivity is a normally distributed trait, like height: plotted in adults it makes the same bell curve, with a mean of about 100 and a standard deviation of about 13 in a sample of 10,000. The examinable reading is the shape — extreme emotional sensitivity is a position in the tail of a normal distribution, not a categorical illness. Temperament is probably set in the first few years of life and largely reflects genetic predisposition, and being emotionally intense is not a problem in itself.

Feature of the temperamentWhat it means
High sensitivity to emotional stimuliLower threshold — emotions are easily triggered
Emotional intensityReactions are more intense
Slow return to emotional baselineReactions last longer

Memory hook: easily triggered → intense → long-lasting.

Impulsivity is a separate biological ingredient, not part of emotional sensitivity. It is very common in BPD and is one of the most heritable personality traits, heritability 20–62%. Patients often have a family history of substance use, especially alcohol, anger problems, and other impulsive behaviour.

The module's own quiz asks you to sort biological from non-biological risk factors. Biological: emotions easily triggered, intense and longer-lasting than average; impulsivity; a family history of impulsive aggression or of substance use problems. Not biological: A+ blood type, extroversion, family history of diabetes — none is a heritable trait of emotion regulation or impulse control.

Social: the invalidating, or "poor fit", environment

Validation means showing that you understand someone's experience; invalidation is the failure to do that — dismissing, ignoring, not responding, being confused by, or criticizing what the person feels.

A very sensitive child experiences emotions as overwhelmingly intense, confusing and painful. The environment that fits is attuned enough to help them cope while still leaving space to sit with distress and learn to manage it. Even well-intentioned parents find this hard: it is easy to feel helpless and frustrated, and a parent who does loses empathy and attunement and responds by giving up, turning away, or criticizing — which is why an invalidating environment does not require a cruel parent.

Examples: not understanding why the child is reacting as they are; getting angry with the child for being emotional; maternal separation of about four months before age 5; neglect and all forms of abuse. Trauma is a severe form of invalidation — childhood sexual abuse runs at 10–20% in the general population against 40–70% in inpatient BPD samples. The teaching example: a child cries when her grandparents leave and is told "Stop that crying or I'll give you something to cry about" — what she learns is that her inner emotional experience must somehow be wrong.

What repeated invalidation does, in order: emotions intensify → the sense of self becomes confused → emotions become hard to identify (alexithymia) → they become so overwhelming that the person looks for a way to escape them. Add the inherited trait of impulsivity and the escape route is impulsive: alcohol and drugs, self-harm or suicide attempts, binge eating, overspending, gambling, shoplifting.

Which social factors count
Risk factors: maternal separation at a young age · neglect · lack of caregiver attunement · reinforcement of emotional outbursts · dismissal of a child's emotions, needs or identity · trauma.
Not risk factors: a caregiver suggesting healthy coping strategies · being able to talk about emotions · invalidation that is then talked about and repaired.
The two traps sit side by side: invalidation followed by repair is protective, while reinforcing emotional outbursts is a risk factor.

How much of each: the transaction

Put two people on the sensitive tail of that bell curve. Person A, only somewhat sensitive at about 2 standard deviations above the mean, develops BPD only with severe invalidation such as trauma. Person B, at the far extreme, can develop BPD with much more subtle invalidation. The principle: the more biological vulnerability, the less environmental invalidation is needed, and the reverse. Risk is the product of two dimensions, never a threshold on either alone. Asked which needed the more severe environment, the answer is Person A, the less sensitive one.

Dandelion childrenOrchid children
Temperament"Easy""Spirited", emotionally intense
EnvironmentDo well in most environments; it takes a large insult to stop them growingFinicky; need the right amount of water and sun
OutcomeRobustThrive in the right environment, wither in the wrong one
BPD riskLowHigh if the environment invalidates

Victoria: the case worked through

You are a family doctor in downtown Toronto. Victoria, 18, the daughter of one of your patients, asks for an urgent appointment. She has been cutting herself and thinking more and more about ending her life: "Please help me doctor, why am I so weird? I feel like I'm going crazy!"

Her mother's account of the early years: as a baby she was colicky and often cried inconsolably, quite unlike her older sister Laura, "such an easy child". As a child and teenager she was "so sensitive and moody", and slammed doors and threw things. When Victoria was upset her mother tried to reassure her that things weren't so bad and told her she was overreacting. It never helped.

Victoria's two halves
Biological: emotionally sensitive temperament · colic · inconsolable crying · temper tantrums.
Social: a mother who offered reassurance, told her she was overreacting, and felt confused, overwhelmed and helpless.
The point that catches people: well-meant reassurance — "things aren't so bad" — is invalidation, because it tells the child her reaction does not match reality. Sympathetic intent does not make it validating.

First year at the University of Toronto. Her boyfriend Mark went to McGill and broke up with her during Frosh Week. She phones and texts him constantly and has asked whether he would stay if she dropped out and moved to Montreal. She feels out of control: she has slept with three different men in her frosh group, regretting it afterward, and is drunk most nights and missing classes. Her mood is usually "up and down"; the break-up leaves her sad for hours or the whole day; she keeps getting very angry with her roommate and regrets it; she still enjoys her new friends and competitive dance. She calls Mark both "the best thing to happen to me" and "the worst person alive". She has had suicidal thoughts on and off since age 12, more frequent since the break-up — wanting to "escape from it all" but not "really wanting to die", no plan, no past attempts. She has been cutting her upper thighs since about age 13, now daily, and wants to stop.

On examination the vitals and physical exam are normal apart from superficial cuts and scarring on the left upper thigh, no infection. On mental status: co-operative and calm, mood "up and down", affect euthymic, congruent, full range and reactive, no hallucinations, urges to self-harm but wanting help, passive suicidal ideation without intent or plan. A euthymic, reactive, full-range affect in the room is what BPD looks like between shifts — it is not evidence against the diagnosis.

The nine criteria: five of nine

The stem, verbatim: a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affect, and marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, as indicated by five (or more) of the following.

Affect — three criteria

  1. Affective instability due to a marked reactivity of mood — intense feelings that come and go in response to external events.
  2. Inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger — frequent displays of temper, recurrent physical fights.
  3. Chronic feelings of emptiness — patients usually know exactly what this means and simply endorse or deny it. Asked where they feel it, they point to their chest or stomach: it appears to be a physical sensation.

Behaviour — two criteria

  1. Impulsivity in at least two potentially self-damaging areas — spending, sex, substance use, reckless driving, binge eating. It excludes suicidal and self-harming behaviour, which belong to criterion 5.
  2. Recurrent suicidal behaviour, gestures or threats, or self-mutilating behaviour — the criterion with the highest associated morbidity and mortality.

Cognition — two criteria

  1. Identity disturbance — a markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self: a completely different person with one group of friends than with another, values and interests shifting to match the company.
  2. Transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms — derealization (things seem unreal) and depersonalization (a spectator on your own life, watching from the ceiling).

Interpersonal — two criteria

  1. A pattern of unstable and intense relationships alternating between the extremes of idealization and devaluation — people are either "good" or "bad" rather than good and bad: splitting.
  2. Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment — threats, pleading, extreme accommodation. Self-harm does not count toward this criterion either.

The domain arithmetic is worth memorizing: affect 3 + behaviour 2 + cognition 2 + interpersonal 2 = 9, threshold 5. That gives 256 different combinations that all meet criteria, which is why two patients with the same diagnosis look nothing alike.

How long the mood shifts last is stated two ways: the criteria list gives a few hours to a few days, the interview teaching minutes to hours. Expect either; both describe short, reactive shifts rather than a sustained episode. If forced to pick, use a few hours to a few days.

Do not confuse BPD affective instability with a mood episode. BPD moods are reactive to an external event, last hours to at most a couple of days, and return to a full-range, reactive baseline in between. A two-week stretch of low mood with anhedonia and early-morning wakening is a depressive episode, however unstable the personality around it. The question that separates them: "Are they usually a reaction to something?"

The mnemonic

ARMS ASIDE — Anger · Relationships unstable · Mood unstable · Self unstable · Abandonment · Suicide or self-harm · Impulsivity · Dissociation and transient paranoia · Emptiness.

How to ask

Start with affective instability — a reasonably sensitive and specific screen for BPD. If a patient shows several behavioural indicators — anger outbursts, self-harm or suicidality, impulsivity such as substance use or disordered eating — work through enough of the rest to see whether five are met.

CriterionHow to ask, and what you are listening for
Affective instability"Do you have intense moods that change rapidly, from neutral to irritated to really anxious?" · "How long do they last?" · "Are they usually a reaction to something?" — you want reactivity, with examples
Anger"Do you have anger outbursts where you yell and scream, throw or break things?"
Chronic emptiness"Do you often feel empty inside?" — a visceral sensation, distinct from loneliness, boredom or dissociation, that drives damaging behaviour
Self-damaging impulsivitySubstances · binge and purge · reckless driving · gambling · shoplifting · spending · impulsive sex regretted afterward — you need ≥2 areas
Suicidality and self-harm"Have you attempted suicide?" · "Have you ever harmed yourself deliberately, like cutting, scratching, headbanging, hitting yourself?"
Identity disturbance"Do you have a solid sense of who you are as a person?" — corroborated by frequent changes of friend group, school or career focus, morals and values
Paranoia and dissociation"When you get really stressed out, do you have strange experiences, like going fuzzy or numb, losing time, feeling like you aren't real?" — stress-related and transient
Abandonment"Do you find yourself frantically trying to stop someone close to you from leaving?" — "leaving" can mean a break-up or just walking out of the room
Unstable relationships"Do you have intense and stormy relationships where you run hot and cold?" — idealization and devaluation

Victoria against the nine criteria

What she describesCriterion it satisfies
Constant phoning and texting; offering to drop out and move to MontrealAbandonment
Three men she is not interested in; drunk most nights; missing classesImpulsivity — two areas, sex and substances
Mood up and down, sad for hours; repeated rages at her roommateAffective instability and anger — two separate criteria
Mark is both the best thing that ever happened and the worst person aliveUnstable relationships (idealization and devaluation)
Suicidal thoughts since 12; cutting since 13, now dailySuicidal behaviour and self-harm — one criterion, counted once

That is six confirmed criteria in a longstanding, impairing pattern, so the answer to "does Victoria have BPD?" is yes. Self, dissociation and emptiness were never assessed and might add more.

Three counting traps in this case
The drinking and the impulsive sex are impulsivity; her cutting cannot be counted there as a third area.
The frantic contact to stop the break-up is abandonment, not unstable relationships — idealizing and devaluing Mark earns that one.
Passive suicidal ideation and cutting share one criterion, counting once.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Self-harm alone is not BPD. It also occurs in adolescent depression and neurodevelopmental disorders, and by itself satisfies exactly one criterion.
  • "Micropsychosis" — brief, stress-related hallucinations or paranoia, criterion 7 — does not by itself indicate a primary psychotic disorder.
  • Onset by early adulthood and a pervasive pattern are part of the stem, and the general personality disorder criteria still have to be met on top of the nine.
  • Worked arithmetic: shoplifting + binge eating + cutting is 2 criteria, not 3 — the first two make one impulsivity criterion, the cutting the self-harm criterion. Self-harm + suicidal threats + spending in one area + anger outbursts is also 2, since one area misses the two-area requirement. Neither is near five: screen the rest.
The two miscounting traps: impulsivity requires two or more areas and excludes self-harm and suicidality, and abandonment excludes self-harm too. Counts get inflated by scoring one patient's cutting under impulsivity, abandonment and self-harm at once. It counts once, under self-harm.
BPD is 5 of 9 criteria across 4 domains — affect 3, behaviour 2, cognition 2, interpersonal 2 — in a pervasive pattern beginning by early adulthood, and it arises when an emotionally sensitive temperament meets an invalidating environment: the greater the biological vulnerability, the less invalidation it takes.

guides.title: Week 40 · 7 BPD Management, Self-harm and Risk Assessment
guides.html:
SLM10–11 · PD Modules 4–5

BPD Management, Self-harm and Risk Assessment

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Psychotherapy over medication, DBT in numbers, the six ways to validate and the in-office distress sequence, then deliberate self-harm: how it differs from suicide, how not to reinforce it, and how to assess and manage risk.

"Doctor, how do you treat BPD?"

Victoria returns: "My emotions are all over the place, I'm always kind of depressed, and I just keep getting overwhelmed." You give her the diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, and she answers: "Wow, I can't believe this is actually a thing — I just thought I was a freak or something. What a relief!" Naming the diagnosis often brings relief, not stigma.

OptionVerdictWhy
Do nothingWrongHelpful treatments for BPD exist
MedicationMaybeNo medication treats BPD itself. Medications may help comorbid conditions — antidepressants where there are significant depressive and anxiety symptoms. Antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are sometimes used, but this is controversial and best left to psychiatrists. Polypharmacy is common in BPD, dangerous or at best unhelpful, and should be avoided. Some patients do well on no medication at all
PsychotherapyCorrectPatients respond both to therapies designed specifically for BPD and to general therapeutic approaches

The same rule holds for personality disorders generally: no medication treats one directly; psychotherapy is the mainstay.

Dialectical behaviour therapy, in numbers

DBT is a structured psychotherapy rooted in CBT, focused less on thoughts and more on behaviour, experiencing emotions and skilful coping. It runs 6–12 months at 1 h per week of individual therapy plus a 2 h per week skills group, and roughly 75% of patients get significant reductions in self-harm, emergency visits and hospital admission days.

The four required modes: individual therapy · skills group · between-session skills coaching by phone · weekly therapist team meetings. The four skill sets: mindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness.

The "D" is dialectics — synthesizing apparent opposites, on the principle that two opposite things can both be true at once, which is what makes the "both-and" statements below work. Other evidence-based psychotherapies for BPD include mentalization-based treatment, transference-focused psychotherapy, schema therapy and good psychiatric management.

The waitlist — where management stops being referral

You explain the options — a specialized BPD or DBT clinic, general therapy, or a psychiatry referral — and that there will be a wait. Victoria becomes upset: "now you say there's nothing to be done for MONTHS!? What am I supposed to do?!" Signs of rising distress: speaking louder and faster, higher pitch, bigger gestures, slapping the arms of the chair. Treating BPD is beyond the medical-school curriculum, but management is more than referral: the three techniques below are DBT-derived and indispensable in the emergency department, or anywhere else you meet an overwhelmed person.

Technique 1 — validation, the six ways

#WaySaid to Victoria
1Show interest — eye contact, don't look bored or distracted, don't look at your computer—
2Reflective statement — summarize what the patient said"You're really upset about the wait lists."
3Mindreading statement — an educated guess at what they think or feel, from what they've said or how they look"You're feeling hugely let down and disappointed — and angry! — because of the waitlists."
4"Makes sense in a context" — use what you know about this individual"Of course this is frustrating, given how long you waited the last time I referred you."
5Normalizing — most people would react the same way"Waiting is one of the biggest problems in our health care system — it IS incredibly frustrating!"
6Be genuine, authentic, cheerleading"I wish this was a problem I could fix! I think you can get through this, and I'll do my best to help."
What not to say. "You are overreacting, please calm down." · "A few months is nothing!" · "I know waiting is frustrating, but it's not that bad. You've done it before." · anything dismissive, patronizing or blandly reassuring.
And "wait lists are a normal part of our system, of course you have to wait" is not normalizing — it normalizes the system, not the patient's reaction. That distinction is the one most often tested.

Why it works, and when it doesn't. People often settle as soon as they are validated, as long as you are sincere, insistent and emphatic — half-hearted validation doesn't help. The mechanism: we get more upset when we feel challenged, doubted or disagreed with, and relax when we feel understood. If validation calms them, you don't need to teach a skill at all. Some people get more upset when validated, focusing harder on painful feelings or feeling confirmed in being right to be upset — that is the moment to ask whether they'd like to learn a coping skill.

Technique 2 — both-and statements

A both-and statement ties your validation to something you can offer:

  • "I hear how hard it is to tolerate having to wait AND I believe you can get through it."
  • "Your overwhelm makes perfect sense AND I'd love to help you get less overwhelmed right now."

Use AND, never but — "but" cancels the validation that came before it.

Technique 3 — suggesting coping skills

  1. Validate, then offer help: "You look really distressed and overwhelmed. I can't fix the wait list, AND maybe I can help you manage how you're feeling right now — would you be willing to try something with me?"
  2. Make specific suggestions — hold something cold (an ice pack) to the temples · breathe together with a longer exhalation · exercise (jumping jacks in your office) · squeeze something very hard. These work fastest because they act on the body: temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation.
  3. Praise them generously for being willing to try, don't be discouraged if the first one or two do nothing, and expect to repeat your validating statements several times throughout.
The sequence to memorize
Validate → both-and → offer help → suggest a skill → suggest another. Worked through: "This is devastating. I see you are feeling really overwhelmed." → "I can't fix the system AND I would like to help you if I can." → "Would you like to try some coping strategies?" → "How about holding an ice pack?" → "OK, if that isn't helpful, let's try slow breathing."

How it branches. If validation lands she may breathe easier but cry harder — validate the sadness too, then offer skills. If she declines skills, back off respectfully and keep validating. If she tries the cold skill, coach her ("just feel the cold on your skin, bring your focus to it") and make sure she knows she can use it at home; if it doesn't help, move to the next one. If she is still distraught and you are out of time, do a brief risk assessment to decide whether she needs the emergency department, then end gently and encourage practice at home.

Your own reactions, and stigma

  • Don't do things for patients that they can do themselves in an effort to be helpful — hold a coaching and cheerleading stance. Ordinary courtesies are fine; think twice before making phone calls they could make themselves.
  • Feeling confused or surprised is common — being followed on social media, being asked many personal questions. Take time to think and consult a colleague.
  • Frustration is common, because change is slow and patients may be hostile, demanding or withdrawn — and it is the source of considerable stigma against BPD among health professionals.
The anti-stigma dialectic
The lives of suicidal people are unbearable as they are currently being lived; people are doing the best they can, they want to improve, and they need to try harder. All of it is true at the same time.

Deliberate self-harm

You're on call. Victoria arrives with her boyfriend: after a fight that day he found she had made five superficial cuts to her wrist with an X-ACTO knife, and thinks she was trying to kill herself. Certify her and keep her in hospital as at imminent risk of suicide? That can only be answered by separating self-harm from suicidal intent.

Deliberate self-harm is deliberately causing tissue damage in the absence of suicidal intent. Common methods: superficial cutting, burning, hitting oneself, head banging, overdosing on prescribed or over-the-counter medications. It serves two functions: to avoid intense affect or anxiety, by supplying an intense stimulus that distracts or promotes endorphin release; and to communicate distress, because people who self-harm often struggle to put pain into words and feel dismissed when they try. Undoing it takes sustained psychotherapy, and the goal is to tolerate feelings without escaping, avoiding or distracting.

Self-harm is not BPD, and not suicide — and none of that makes it minor

  • Self-harm is one of the BPD criteria but is not pathognomonic — it also occurs in adolescents with depression and in neurodevelopmental disorders. Even when it isn't BPD it marks difficulty regulating emotions, so consider a therapy referral anyway.
  • If a patient says they cut to avoid emotion or relieve stress and were not trying to die, they are most likely telling the truth. Self-harm frequently occurs without imminent suicide risk.
  • But self-harm and suicidal ideation or attempts often co-occur in the same person, and self-harm raises suicide risk sharply: the 1-year rate after self-harm is 439.1 per 100,000 person-years — 37.2 times the general-population rate of 11.8 per 100,000.
  • Accidental death is a real pathway: too many pills, or cutting deeper than intended and hitting an artery.

Avoiding reinforcement

Reinforcement is a consequence that makes a behaviour happen more often. For most patients self-harm is reinforced by internal relief from painful emotion; for some, also by soothing and care from other people. Calling that "attention-seeking" is unfair and judgmental — the intent is rarely to get attention — but attention that follows self-harm, positive or negative, may still make it more frequent.

In the acute setting, say while suturing the cuts, too infantilizing sounds like "You poor thing, you must REALLY be in pain to do this to yourself"; too hostile sounds like "And what were you hoping this would accomplish?" or "I don't know why I'm bothering, since you'll just do this again next week." The right stance is kind, respectful, neutral and matter-of-fact, with no less civility than you'd show any other patient — and note that anger and contempt reinforce too, because they are still attention.

Longer term: the sooner you give warm, caring contact after self-harm, the more likely you are to reinforce it. What helps is genuine warmth when they have not recently self-harmed, and genuine disappointment or less warmth — not punitive anger — when they have. Increasing appointment frequency during a crisis can reinforce crisis behaviour; hold the frequency steady, or raise it only on condition that they stay away from self-harm and suicide threats.

Assessment and management

Assessing the self-harm — five steps. 1. Take the history of self-harm: age it started, methods, frequency, precipitants. 2. Ask explicitly about intent at the moment of the self-harm. 3. Ask about suicidal ideation — but don't presume they are suicidal. 4. Screen for the other BPD criteria. 5. Remember not everyone who self-harms has BPD, adolescents especially — but self-harm is a dangerous way to avoid emotion, so arrange a diagnostic assessment and some form of treatment regardless.

Managing the presentation — four steps. 1. ABCs and medical treatment first. 2. Suicide risk assessment. 3. Encourage mental health follow-up. 4. Refer to psychiatry whenever unsure or wanting a second opinion.

What that yields with Victoria: started at 13; cutting and scratching, 2–3 times a month; precipitants usually fights with her boyfriend, sometimes other interactions leaving her feeling rejected or alone; intent relief from awful feelings; suicidal thoughts sometimes, but not this time — while cutting she did not want to die. Her suicidal thoughts come without intent and she is future-oriented. The modules describe her history slightly differently — onset at 11 in one and 13 in two others, daily cutting in the post-break-up period against 2–3 times a month at this visit — so use the figure the stem gives and don't mix them.

Admission is not the safe default
Many patients with chronic, fluctuating suicidal ideation do not benefit from psychiatric admission. Hospitalization can become an escape behaviour that undermines coping in ordinary life, and a potent reinforcer of suicidal thinking, communication and behaviour. That judgement is usually the psychiatrist's to make.

Restricting means — one of the best ways to reduce risk

If a person has to wait, think or problem-solve to reach the means, the urge may pass before they act on it.

MeansWhat to do
HeightsHigh-rise? Balcony? Someone can lock or block it
Medications at homeReduce the supply as far as possible — nobody needs 100 tablets of acetaminophen at home
Sharps and firearmsSome knives are needed for cooking — "but do you really need 10?" Weapons ideally off the premises; if not, locked, key inaccessible, ammunition locked separately
Your own prescribingSmall amounts, 1–2 weeks at a time; ask about stockpiling and whether they are actually taking it
Dangerous medicationsAsk specifically about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen and other people's medications, such as cardiac drugs

Victoria's disposition — the worked answer

Is her risk high or low? Low. She has suicidal thoughts but won't act on them, has no current suicidal intent, and is planning to go to a friend's party — future-oriented. The correct next steps are discharge, therapy referral, crisis lines and skills, and psychoeducation for the partner:

OptionVerdict and reason
Discharge homeYes — not at imminent risk of suicide; she does not need hospital
Certify or admit herNo — she does not intend to act on the thoughts; admission is an unnecessary intervention for self-harm
Refer to therapyYes — the best intervention for learning healthy coping
Tell her contemptuously to manage her own feelings, or warmly invite her back any time she's upsetNo to both — hostility is unprofessional and reinforces the behaviour, and an open invitation produces repeated unnecessary visits. Teach skills; keep the hospital available for emergencies
Crisis lines and distress-tolerance skillsYes — crisis lines are a source of validation; skills let her cope independently
Psychoeducation for the partner or familyYes — helps him feel less panicked and suggest therapy instead of insisting she come to hospital
Two traps that look like kindness. "Come back any time you're upset" sounds caring but reinforces crisis-driven emergency use — the correct wording is "for emergencies". And an overly soothing response while suturing is as much a problem as a hostile one: both reinforce. Separately, family therapy is not one of DBT's four modes — the fourth is between-session phone coaching.

Cheat sheet

ItemKey fact
Three clustersA odd/eccentric · B dramatic/erratic · C anxious/fearful
Diagnosing BPD5 of 9 criteria, Cluster B
First-line managementPsychotherapy, BPD-specific or general; no medication treats BPD itself — treat comorbidity only, avoid polypharmacy
DBT in one line6–12 months, 1 h individual + 2 h group weekly, about 75% improved. Modes: individual · group · phone coaching · team meeting. Skills: mindfulness · distress tolerance · emotion regulation · interpersonal effectiveness
Self-harm definedDeliberate tissue damage without suicidal intent; functions are to avoid intense affect and to communicate distress
Suicide risk after self-harm439.1 vs 11.8 per 100,000 person-years — 37.2 times, at 1 year
Risk management stepsABCs and medical care → suicide risk assessment → mental health follow-up → psychiatry if unsure
Refer for psychotherapy rather than reaching for medication; validate sincerely before you offer a skill, and use AND rather than but; and treat self-harm as real without treating it as an emergency — neutral tone, an explicit question about intent, means restriction and a therapy referral, with admission left to the psychiatrist's judgement.

guides.title: Week 40 · 8 The Psychiatric Interview, Mental Status Examination and Case Report (ICE CS2)
guides.html:
Clinical skills · ICE CS2

The Psychiatric Interview, Mental Status Examination and Case Report (ICE CS2)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The ICE CS2 student guide end to end: the interview road map, the 33 process steps, every history domain, the 13 MSE categories with their descriptors, the session format and the MedSIS case-report rubric.

The two instruments

Psychiatry deals with disorders of behaviour, thought, emotion and motivation, which like any medical illness may have physical, social or psychological causes or complications. The psychiatric history is what the patient reports; the mental state examination is what you observe at the interview — behaviour, appearance, emotion, consciousness and memory, speech, thought and perception, domain for domain. Together they let you reach a diagnosis, offer a prognosis and treat. Interviewing is a technique, not a talent: it asks only for interest, attention and practice, and breaks into behavioural steps you can name, observe and improve.

The interview, step by step

  1. Greet the patient, explain the set-up, give your name and that you are a medical student, ask their name.
  2. Ask their understanding of why the interview is happening; explain if they do not know.
  3. Say how much time is available, then open with open questions, so the story comes in the patient's words.
  4. Listen; let the patient finish without interruption, leave silence to think.
  5. Once the chief complaint is done, ask openly if there is anything else.
  6. Facilitate — repeat or paraphrase to prompt more, and follow verbal clues hinting at unexplored problems.
  7. Check out non-verbal clues — body language, tone of voice, facial expression, affect — that reinforce or contradict the words.
  8. Ask their feelings about what they describe, and separately their thoughts.
  9. Move from open to closed questions when the account stops being coherent, relevant or consistent: resolve ambiguities, clear up what you do not follow.
  10. Press for precision — anything datable or quantifiable. Ask them to define obscure words; avoid jargon yourself.
  11. Ask single, brief questions, one at a time; avoid leading questions. Show calm interest in emotionally loaded material — suicide, domestic abuse, money, sex, death and dying — and raise those topics yourself when clues suggest relevance.
  12. Keep track of the time, avoid repetition, stay flexibly on task with your changes of direction clear to the patient, redirect tactfully.
  13. Raise sensitive topics before the end, never as an afterthought. Then summarize briefly, convey your understanding of the concerns, validation and where appropriate hope, and thank the patient for their time. Useful phrases: "Help me to understand…", "Let's work together to…", "In the interest of time, I may ask more quickly".

How to do it, not just what to do

Do not rush to talk, ask or explain. It is more efficient to let the patient disclose and explain than to poke with one question after another, which signals that asking matters more to you than listening. A clinical interview should not feel like an interrogation. A patient who feels judged or patronized closes off, leaving you to pick through every possibility yourself; go back to open questions, name the non-verbal clue you can see, and leave silence. On empathy: paying attention is the first step; showing that you are paying attention is the second — both observable, both scored.

The core loop, and two rules
1 Slow down, stop, think · 2 look, notice · 3 listen · 4 prompt for more · 5 probe what you do not understand — then re-iterate, each pass bringing you closer to a diagnosis you can build a safe, practical plan on. Replace words carrying a negative connotation: "commit suicide" → die by suicide, "drug abuse" → drug use. And never interview from a checklist — use it after; do not confuse the order of presenting a case with the sequence of information-gathering.

What to ask — the history domains

Five things are the minimum: the reason the patient is here, the course of the problems, their severity, what plausibly caused the illness, what affects management and prognosis.

DomainWhat to ask
Reason for the visitCurrent problem(s) · hopes or expectations of treatment · the patient's own view of the cause
Course of the illnessOnset of this episode · precipitants · chronology, fluctuations, progression · treatment of it · past problems, treatment or attempts
Severity — functionImpact on patient and family in four domains: personal care and survival · family · occupational (paid, volunteer, student, homemaker) · social
Severity — riskSuicide · other deliberate self-harm · violence to others · inability to look after oneself · self-neglect · neglect of dependents
Personal and social circumstancesPartner · family · others · housing · occupation · finances · legal involvement · leisure · recent changes or losses · support available
Active physical factorsActive medical problems · medications (which, why, dose) · alcohol or drug use, and how much
Systematic enquiryScreens for cognition, hallucinations or delusions, mood, anxiety

A full developmental history belongs in a psychiatric assessment, but at this stage first get the problem, its biopsychosocial context and its impact — even experienced clinicians leave the early life story for a later interview.

Screening questions

Depression. "Have you ever had 2 weeks or more when you felt sad or low, most of the day, nearly every day?" — same stem for lost interest. Anchor one episode (worst, most recent, first, longest), then screen suicidal ideation, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, sleep. Mania. "Have you had an unusually high mood for many days in a row? How many days?" and "Did you have increased energy? Were you more active?" Then grandiosity, reduced sleep, talkativeness, goal-directed activity, flight of ideas, distractibility.

Anxiety. Generalized — do you worry about multiple things, and is the worry hard to control? Panic — do intense physical symptoms come on suddenly? Agoraphobia — do you avoid being in public? Social — do social situations provoke anxiety or fear of judgement? Specific phobia — things (heights, closed spaces, animals) you fear or avoid?

Delusions run off one stem, "Has it ever seemed that…": people are after you (persecutory) · an outside force controls your actions (control) · others know your thoughts (mind reading) · you have special abilities (grandiose) · things happen because of you (reference) · thoughts are put in (insertion) or taken out (withdrawal) · your body has changed (somatic). In depression with psychosis they tend to be mood congruent. For hallucinations, ask about hearing things others do not hear, then quality, inside or outside the head, commentary and command, then visual. Also screen obsessive-compulsive and post-traumatic symptoms.

The suicide ladder
1 "Has life seemed so stressful that you think about death or suicide?" → 2 "Are you thinking about ways you would end your life?" → 3 "Have you prepared or acquired the means?" → 4 "How would you describe your level of intent?" → 5 "Have you attempted suicide in the past?" → 6 acute versus chronic → 7 active (plans) versus passive (thoughts of death) → 8 "What are some reasons for staying alive?" Order: ideation → method → means → intent → past attempts, then classification, then protective factors.

The range of problems, and how a diagnosis is built

Psychiatric problems span symptoms and predicaments: aggressive or agitated behaviour; self-injury and suicidality; substance misuse; physical illness (either the cause or the result of psychiatric symptoms); cognitive problems; delusions and hallucinations; depressed or elated mood; anxiety, phobias, obsessions; somatoform and dissociative problems; fatigue, sleep, eating and sexual problems; poor self-care; isolation and conflict — then predicaments, not symptoms: living conditions, work, leisure.

Your goal is a diagnosis in order to arrive at a plan of management. A working diagnosis needs classification of the symptoms and signs — the illness; the context in which they are understood — the predicament; and the underlying pathophysiology where findable — the disease. The plan must be biopsychosocial, feasible, and must mitigate any safety concerns. Course matters as much as cross-section and can only be discovered from the history: how dangerous the condition is, how great the impairment, the psychosocial context, the physical factors, and who the person is.

Think of the major disorders as a hierarchy — no moral implication, purely diagnostic. Physical conditions, disease or drug-induced, sit uppermost: hallmark confusion, possibly every feature of the rungs below, and identifiable pathology makes them most treatable. The psychoses sit below: impaired reality-testing, delusions and hallucinations, unlikely to show confusion. Depression and anxiety sit lowest: affective symptoms without confusion or impaired reality-testing. Disorders higher up often feature the symptoms of those below, while lower ones rarely show the signs of those above — so delusions plus confusion push you up the ladder, towards a physical or drug-induced cause. Always ask about concurrent substance use and symptom intensity when abstinent.

The mental status examination

The mental status exam is the physical exam of psychiatry: a summary of your observations which, with the history, gives a diagnosis. Pressured speech, distractibility and labile affect point to mania; dysphoria, delayed thought processing and poverty of speech the other way.

DomainWhat to describe, with usable descriptors
AppearanceApparent versus chronological age, gender, heritage; posture, grooming, dress, habitus; eye contact, expression. Untidy, gaunt
AttitudePolite, collaborative, uncooperative, guarded, evasive, hostile; reliability as a historian, ease of rapport
BehaviourRestless, hyperactive, slowed, withdrawn; gait, psychomotor slowing or agitation, mannerisms, tics, dyskinesia
SpeechRate (normal, pressured, slowed), rhythm, volume, tone; quantity, spontaneity, latency. Monotonous, sparse
Thought formOrganized and goal-directed, circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, word salad; flight of ideas, blocking, incoherent
Sensorium and cognitionLevel of consciousness; orientation to name, place, time; attention, memory, intellect; formal screen if needed. Drowsy, disorientated, forgetful
MoodSubjective — as the patient reports it, scaled 0–10, 0 = worst, 10 = well. Anxious, depressed, elated
AffectObjective — as you observe it: quality (euthymic, depressed, elevated, anxious, irritable), range (full, restricted, flat, blunted), stability (fixed to labile), congruence with mood and content
Thought contentThemes, preoccupations, over-valued ideas, delusions, obsessions, suicidal and homicidal ideation with intent and plan
PerceptionHallucinations reported — auditory, visual, olfactory, tactile — and observed responding to internal stimuli
Insight and judgementEach graded none or impaired · partial · intact. Insight — realizing you have a mental health concern and its implications. Judgement — recent behaviour around safety, functioning and treatment; impulsive, lewd
The two pairs examiners quote at you. Mood is subjective, affect is objective — mood is what the patient tells you, affect is what you see, and you say whether the two are congruent. Insight is recognizing the illness and its implications; judgement is recent behaviour around safety, functioning and treatment. Sources print 11, 12 or 13 headings depending on how Behaviour and Speech are folded in — learn the domains, not the count, and always include attitude.

The sessions and the case report

Four four-hour sessions, each running group discussion led by the preceptor → interviews of a standardized patient → group feedback. In the first the tutor demonstrates on a real patient while you interview a standardized patient; later sessions run two interviews, feedback after each. Outcomes run in order: the structure of an assessment and the history/mental state distinction; an interview's process, then its content, then the organization of the mental state examination. Sessions are mandatory — missing one, even with approval, needs a written make-up, and not notifying the tutor and site coordinator in advance may draw a poor professionalism mark.

Submit a write-up of your own interview within two weeks of the final psychiatric session, in four parts: history, mental state, diagnostic impression, plan of management. Satisfactory is required to pass, and interview skills are examined in the OSCE in the global assessment of every station, not only psychiatry ones. The mark runs on five points with the middle one, meets expectations, as the pass; in every criterion the jump to the top is from completeness to synthesis:

  • Data collection — enough to identify the major problem, and beyond that this patient's psychosocial context.
  • Language — terms used appropriately and every observation filed in the right category: never report a thought-content finding as an affect finding.
  • Approach and global assessment — the problem recognized with an accurate description of the illness; a complete history and mental state, succinct, rising to synthesis.
  • Summary — the encounter in 2–3 sentences naming the most pertinent historical and mental state findings, plus an attempted diagnostic impression; coverage of every history domain above and the four screens.

The history template, as a checklist

  • Introduction — name and role · purpose · circumstances · limits of confidentiality. Identifying data — age, gender and pronouns · living situation · relationship status · children · income and occupation · inpatient or outpatient, voluntary or not.
  • Chief concern — "Tell me about the concerns you've had recently": subjective report, symptom, duration.
  • History of present concern — context (events, stressors, losses, precipitants) · symptoms by onset, duration, progression, intensity, with "describe what that's like" · fluctuation by day, cycle, season · impact on daily activities and on work, social and family functioning · supports, treatments, coping · longitudinal course (first onset, worst episode, typical duration) · last period of wellness · personality change when unwell · beliefs about cause, hopes of treatment.
  • Review of systems — mood · anxiety · psychosis · compulsions, post-traumatic symptoms, disordered eating. Risk — suicide, self-harm, self-neglect · aggression · dependents · safe driving and cooking.
  • Past psychiatric history — diagnoses and contacts · emergency visits · hospitalizations · suicide attempts (number, severity, medical intervention, most recent) · self-harm · charges · treatments, with effectiveness and side effects.
  • Substance use — tobacco, cannabis, alcohol, stimulants, hallucinogens, prescriptions, caffeine, plus gambling and online use · first, typical and last use, abstinence · withdrawal including seizures and delirium tremens · motivation to change.
  • Past medical history — especially endocrine and neurological (seizures, head injuries) · pregnancies · surgeries. Medications — name, dose, frequency · contraceptives · over-the-counter and herbal · adherence, side effects · allergies.
  • Family psychiatric history — diagnoses, treatments, hospitalizations, attempts, substance use.
  • Past personal history — birthplace, heritage, religion · family members and the quality of those relationships · trauma — verbal, physical and sexual abuse, neglect, domestic violence · prenatal and perinatal · early childhood (milestones, temperament, caregivers) · school age (academics, socializing, bullying) · sexuality · adulthood · strengths: hobbies, meaning, accomplishments, hopes.

Commonly omitted steps

The steps students drop most are not the obvious courtesies — greeting, naming yourself a medical student and avoiding jargon are not on this list.
  • Asking the patient's understanding of the interview; stating how much time there is.
  • Letting the patient finish, leaving silence, asking for anything else, checking out non-verbal clues.
  • Moving open → closed when open questions stop working, and pressing for datable detail.
  • Raising loaded topics yourself, not saving them for the end; summarizing; thanking.
  • Risk beyond suicide: neglect of dependents; safe driving and cooking.
Interview for a diagnosis so you can make a safe, practical plan: classify the illness, discern the predicament, look for the disease — then write a plan that is biopsychosocial, feasible and mitigates every safety concern found.
