Lecture 1 · Byrne

Introduction to Psychiatry (Byrne, Lecture 1)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What psychiatry is, how a disorder is separated from ordinary distress, the DSM-5 categories and their limits, and what makes a person vulnerable — diathesis–stress, ACEs and attachment.

What psychiatry is, and why every physician needs it

Psychiatry is the branch of medicine focused on the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of mental, emotional and behavioural disorders, at the intersection of biology, psychology and social context. It reaches every specialty: 1 in 9 primary care encounters involves a mental health condition (up to 30% of family practice visits), and psychiatric comorbidity worsens other outcomes — cancer patients carry higher all-cause mortality.

  • 1 in 8 people worldwide live with a mental disorder; mental disorders account for about 1 in 6 years lived with disability.
  • Canada: about 12 deaths by suicide per day and 4,500 per year; rates 3× higher in men; suicide is the second leading cause of death at ages 15–34.
  • Men die by suicide more; women self-harm more, where self-harm means non-suicidal self-injury.
  • About 30% of people meet criteria for an anxiety disorder at some point in life, a first hint that psychopathology is continuous with ordinary experience.

Stigma, media and misinformation

  • In high-income settings only one third of people with depression get treatment.
  • Three levels of stigma: individual (internalized shame), interpersonal (fear of judgement), structural (racism, barriers to time off work). Internalized stigma predicts worse symptoms, poorer adherence and earlier discontinuation of antidepressants.
  • Awareness campaigns lower stigma, but most online content is not clinical: of the top 1,000 #MentalHealth videos only 19.1% came from a licensed professional and one third were misleading, and a 2022 UBC study found 52% of the 100 most popular ADHD videos on TikTok misleading. A viral "visible signs of depression" clip listed no actual DSM criteria for depression.
  • Werther effect (harmful): detailed, sensationalized or romanticized coverage of suicide raises suicidal behaviour by social learning and imitation — the discriminator in a vignette being the glamourizing content of the exposure. Named for Goethe's 1774 The Sorrows of Young Werther. Evidence: about 195 extra deaths among US youth 10–17 in the 3 months after 13 Reasons Why, and a 10% rise in US suicides after Robin Williams' death.
  • Papageno effect (protective): coverage of alternatives to suicide, coping and recovery lowers ideation through hope, less stigma, modelled coping and help-seeking. Named for Papageno in Mozart's The Magic Flute.

What counts as a mental disorder

A syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotional regulation or behaviour, reflecting a dysfunction in psychological, biological or developmental processes. Three qualifiers sit under it: the condition causes significant psychological pain or functional impairment; it is not an expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss (grief after a death); and symptoms arise from an underlying abnormality rather than purely from external stress. The discriminator for "this is a disorder" is functional impairment, not the stressor or comorbid history, and the axes that decide it are frequency, intensity and duration.

One subtlety: that expectable-response exclusion belongs to the general definition of a mental disorder and is not a DSM criterion for depression. A patient meeting nine of nine depressive symptoms after a catastrophe anyone would react to may still be better called an adjustment disorder.

Categorical classification and the DSM-5 map

DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association) and ICD-11 (World Health Organization, used more internationally) are both categorical: diagnoses are qualitatively distinct from normal functioning and from each other, and discrete, so you either meet criteria or you do not. The categories: mood (depression, bipolar I and II) · anxiety (GAD, panic, phobias) · obsessive-compulsive and related (OCD, hoarding, body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania, excoriation) · trauma and stressor-related (PTSD, acute stress disorder) · psychotic · personality · neurodevelopmental (autism, ADHD, intellectual disability) · substance-related and addictive (including gambling) · eating · somatic symptom · neurocognitive (delirium, dementias).

Worked case 1: panic disorder

A 20-year-old man, mother died last year. Daily panic attacks for 9 months, calling EMS weekly for chest pain: abrupt chest pain, sweating, shortness of breath, tremor, sense of doom. He lives in fear of further attacks, will not leave home alone, avoids crowded and enclosed spaces. No suicidal ideation, no substances, family history of anxiety.

A. Recurrent unexpected panic attacks — an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms: palpitations · sweating · trembling · shortness of breath · choking · chest pain · nausea · dizziness · chills or heat sensations · paresthesias · derealization or depersonalization · fear of losing control · fear of dying. B. At least one attack followed by 1 month or more of persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences, and/or significant maladaptive behaviour change. C and D. Not due to a substance or another medical condition, and not better explained by another disorder.

He meets criteria: four or more symptoms, unexpected attacks peaking quickly, and both worry and avoidance far beyond a month. Management as written: fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning plus CBT with in vivo and interoceptive exposure. It responds well, but the diagnosis says what he has, not why.

Worked case 2: the depressive episode that isn't

A 23-year-old woman managing a clothing store full time. Low self-esteem since childhood, avoids closeness and promotions. Periods of sadness that come on intensely and last at most an hour, once or twice weekly. Binge drinking, no suicidal ideation, no missed work or social events.

A major depressive episode requires 5 or more symptoms in the same 2-week period, a change from previous functioning: (1) depressed mood most of the day nearly every day; (2) markedly diminished interest or pleasure; (3) significant unintended weight loss or gain; (4) insomnia or hypersomnia; (5) psychomotor agitation or retardation; (6) fatigue; (7) worthlessness or excessive guilt; (8) reduced concentration or indecisiveness; (9) recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, or an attempt or specific plan.

The gate most people drop. Five of nine is not enough on its own: at least one of the five must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure. An option reading "any 5 of 9 over two weeks" is wrong for that reason, and a vignette with five neurovegetative symptoms but preserved mood and interest does not make the diagnosis.

She does not meet criteria, on two grounds: no functional impairment, and failure of the duration requirement, since an hour or two of sadness is not an episode, which runs at least two weeks, day in and day out. The pairing is deliberate: panic meets criteria, depression does not, and she is still suffering.

Four limitations of categorical diagnosis

  1. Arbitrary diagnostic thresholds. Four of nine is not an episode, five is. Dr. Byrne stressed the cost: in the United States, failing to meet criteria can mean no insurance coverage, even for an impaired four-symptom patient.
  2. Comorbidity. A patient labelled with GAD, borderline personality disorder, depression and ADHD at once is still one brain, and more likely one process manifesting as different symptoms.
  3. Heterogeneity. Same label, different patients: one sleeps not at all, has lost 50 lb and is catatonic; another binge eats and sleeps 14 hours a day.
  4. Subthreshold illness. Impairment without a diagnosis; limitation 1 from the patient's side.

The lecture put the symptom combinations for a depressive episode at roughly 256 while the commonly published figure is 227; expect either, and hold the point rather than the number, that one label covers hundreds of presentations. In the classic stem a patient with clear impairment meets only three of nine criteria: he is suffering but falls below the cutoff, which the WFQ keys as arbitrary cutoffs excluding clinically significant cases.

The dimensional alternative

  • Traits and symptoms lie on a continuum; disorders are exaggerated, inflexible or dysregulated versions of normal traits, and differences are quantitative rather than qualitative. Narcissism and neuroticism are measurable and normally distributed, partly heritable, partly shaped by early development.
  • HiTOP and RDoC are the formal frameworks: complex, hard to apply at the bedside, used for research, not clinical practice.
  • Re-read the second patient dimensionally (low self-worth, hopelessness, alcohol misuse) and there is no diagnosis but real suffering, plus a plan: targeted psychotherapy for self-esteem and psychoeducation about alcohol. A categorical reading discharges her with nothing.

Why the brain is vulnerable

Evolutionary psychology. Traits that look maladaptive now were possibly adaptive in ancestral environments; evolution selects for reproductive fitness, not happiness or health; and some emotional responses are normally adaptive systems that become excessive, persistent or contextually mismatched. Anxiety once aided survival by avoiding predators; modern stressors such as academic pressure activate the same systems with no physical threat present, producing anxiety disorders when dysregulated, which is how the WFQ keys it.

Diathesis–stress: mental illness = predisposition (diathesis) + stressor. Diathesis is set by biological, psychological and social history and is a sliding scale, not a binary switch: high diathesis needs very little stress to produce symptoms, low diathesis can absorb major stress without illness. Stressors named: bereavement · job loss · divorce · academic pressure · physical illness · substance use · chronic discrimination.

The diathesis–stress graph, and the sibling question
Predisposition runs low to high along the x-axis, stress up the y-axis, and a diagonal dashed line divides "disorder not manifested" (lower left) from "disorder manifested" (upper right). So the same stress crosses the line at high predisposition but not at low, the line is a threshold, not a point, and the model is continuous in both axes.

When a woman with chronic anxiety asks why her sibling, raised in the same house, is well: diathesis–stress interactions vary between individuals. Siblings are not genetic copies, and the same household is not the same environment. The model is taught clinically because the risk factors you map in the interview are the things you treat.

The biopsychosocial model, proposed by George Engel in 1977, holds that biological, psychological and social factors interact dynamically to converge on health; in psychiatry culture is added as a fourth arm.

Predisposing factors

Biological

  • Heritability: anxiety in aunts and uncles raises your own risk.
  • Inherited temperamental traits. Temperament means innate traits influencing early interaction with the world: present from infancy, biologically based, foundational to personality, and distinct from learned behaviour and from attachment.
  • Epigenetic change from early-life stress, such as DNA methylation, altering gene expression and raising risk.
  • Neurodevelopmental abnormalities in childhood.
Do not confuse epigenetic with inherited. DNA methylation is an epigenetic mark; the short and long alleles of the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) are inherited sequence variation, not an epigenetic change. The two get blurred in teaching and in exam distractors.

Social: the ACE study

In 1995 a Kaiser and CDC team mailed a retrospective questionnaire to over 17,000 insured adults; adversities were tallied, each "yes" scoring one point, and records were then followed prospectively, linking ACE dose to later morbidity. The 10 items cover, before the 18th birthday: neglect · loss of a parent · household mental illness or suicide attempt · household substance use · domestic violence · household incarceration · verbal abuse · physical abuse · feeling unloved · unwanted sexual contact. More than 60% of adults report at least one ACE: about 64% with 1 or more, 12% with 4 or more.

Mental health, 4+ ACEsRiskPhysical health, 4+ ACEsRisk
Major depression~4.4×Ischemic heart disease~2.2×
Anxiety disorders~3.7×COPD~3.9×
Drug use disorder>10×Cancer diagnosis~1.9×
Suicide attemptup to 12×Adult obesity~1.5–2× odds

The finding is dose–response: higher score, higher risk across outcomes. Those physical outcomes are a selection — diabetes belongs on the list too. Childhood adversity shapes risk for both mental and physical disorders in adulthood.

Protective factors: "good enough" is not "frictionless"
Not all children with high ACE scores become ill: each additional positive childhood experience lowers adult depression risk by 26%. Winnicott's "good enough" parent means ordinary, non-ideal care suffices for healthy development, and its complement is optimal frustration: children need some adversity to build resilience. An option offering "shield the child from all adversity" as a protective factor is wrong on this lecture's own terms.

Psychological: attachment

Insecure attachment and adverse early caregiving raise the risk of psychopathology across diagnostic categories. John Bowlby showed the infant is biologically wired to seek proximity to a caregiver providing food and protection, humans being born so underdeveloped that an uncared-for infant dies. Harlow's rhesus monkeys were given a wire mother holding the milk and a soft cloth mother with none, the prediction being preference for the feeding mother. The result is the opposite: the infant clings to the cloth mother and visits the wire only briefly to feed, so contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment.

Securely attached children use the caregiver as a safe base and explore freely; insecurely attached children fear exploring because they are unsure they can return, with later mistrust and difficulty forming relationships. Roughly one third of people are insecurely attached, two thirds securely, across three insecure types.

  • Inconsistent or intrusive care → anxious. Hypervigilance to rejection, chronic worry, constant reassurance-seeking; GAD, panic, somatic symptom disorder.
  • Emotionally unavailable or rejecting care → avoidant. Deactivation, alexithymia, compulsive self-sufficiency, difficulty trusting; substance misuse, restricting eating disorders, schizoid traits.
  • Maltreatment or a frightening caregiver → disorganized. Fragmented self-concept, dissociation, affect lability; borderline personality disorder, complex PTSD, self-harm.

Both classic vignettes key to avoidant: the adult with alcohol use disorder whose parents never showed affection, and the child who hides when upset from a caregiver who ignores her crying. That child's behaviour is an adaptation, not a deficit: hiding distress works when showing it makes the caregiver angry.

Bias and culture in diagnosis

Norms for emotion, behaviour and spirituality differ across societies, and clinicians can misread culturally normative behaviour as psychopathology: visions or voices during prayer mistaken for psychosis. Bias also runs along race: Black patients in North America are more likely to receive a schizophrenia diagnosis than a mood disorder diagnosis even when symptom profiles are similar. Six strategies: cultural humility · structured tools, specifically the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview · elicit the patient's perspective · collaborate with interpreters, cultural liaisons and community healers · education on idioms of distress and culture-bound syndromes · avoid assumptions. Where a stem gives a cultural mismatch, the keyed move is to explore the patient's explanatory model of illness and arrange follow-up, not to diagnose immediately.

Off the exam: the introduction to nosology module, withdrawn and carrying no questions, and the additional-resources material. Being told not to memorize the panic criteria as printed, or to be merely familiar with the category list, is about rote recall rather than the concept — the panic threshold and the disorder-versus-distress discriminators are still tested.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Disorder versus distress: the discriminator is functional impairment, decided on frequency, intensity and duration, not the presence of a stressor.
  • Depression gate: 5 of 9 over 2 weeks and at least one of depressed mood or anhedonia. Panic: at least 4 of 13 peaking within minutes, plus a month or more of worry or behaviour change, not attacks alone.
  • Impairment with a sub-cutoff count keys to arbitrary thresholds and subthreshold illness, never comorbidity or heterogeneity; symptom tracking works in either system. Wording: "qualitatively distinct, discrete" is categorical, "quantitative, exaggerated normal traits" dimensional.
  • Temperament is innate from infancy, not learned behaviour and not attachment.
Mental illness sits at the intersection of biology, psychology and social context. DSM and ICD categories are useful but imperfect maps: risk is continuous, running vulnerability × stress, so a patient can be impaired and still fall below a cutoff. Development, attachment and evolved emotional systems explain vulnerability; culture, stigma and bias shape who gets diagnosed and treated.

Lecture 2 · Byrne

Assessment, Diagnosis and Formulation (Byrne, Lecture 2)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The psychiatric interview, alliance and empathy, the ROS mnemonics, the ASEPTIC mental status exam, and the 4 P's biopsychosocial formulation worked through on one case.

1 · The psychiatric interview

The psychiatric assessment is structurally the same as any other specialty's history. What differs is the depth of the personal and developmental history, a routine safety screen, and the MSE standing in for the physical exam. Seven minutes in emergency, an hour in clinic.

Four goals: understand the concern; build an alliance (patients disclose difficult material only if they trust you); assess diagnosis and safety; agree a plan. A personal or hostile question is answered briefly, redirected, and read as data about the patient.

The safety screen is asked at every psychiatric interview: suicidal thoughts · violent thoughts towards others · driving safety · child safety — three of which return as the exceptions to confidentiality. Keep a clear exit path, sit closest to the door, and if the patient becomes agitated, stop the interview. Psychosis carries roughly twice the risk of violence.

Opening: introduce yourself · say what the interaction is and how long it will take · review the limits of confidentiality with every patient, every time — confidential except where the law obliges doctors to act on safety: a threat to someone's life, a child's care, or driving safety. The warning must come before the disclosure, not after.

2 · Alliance and empathy

Alliance: the patient must feel the evaluation is a joint effort, that you are genuinely interested, and that you care — built by four behaviours: listen without interrupting · acknowledge distress · explain your questions · agree on priorities.

Empathy is understanding what the patient is thinking and feeling — putting yourself in their place while maintaining objectivity; the guard on the other side is over-identification. Verbally, "that must have been very difficult for you"; nonverbally, raised eyebrows, leaning in, nodding. Wiseman's four qualities: perspective taking · staying out of judgement · recognizing emotion in others · communicating it back. Empathy fuels connection, sympathy drives disconnection, and rarely does an empathic response begin with "at least".

3 · The interview outline

Fifteen headings, in order: Identifying Data · Chief Complaint and Reason for Referral · History of Present Illness · Review of Systems · Risk Assessment · Substance Use · Past Psychiatric History · Past Medical History · Medications · Allergies · Family History · Developmental and Social History · Mental Status Examination · Physical Examination · Collateral.

Identifying data is longer in psychiatry than anywhere else because it contextualizes the HPI and feeds the Social column of the formulation: age, sex, gender identity, pronouns, ethnicity and culture, relationships and children, occupation, education, income, living situation. Chief complaint — the reason for presenting, in the patient's own words. HPI: onset, duration, progression · precipitating stressors · symptom clusters (mood, anxiety, psychosis, sleep, appetite, cognition) · functional impact · suicidal or homicidal ideation · insight · coping.

4 · Review of systems — the four core screens

Depression · mania/hypomania · psychosis · anxiety at essentially every assessment, with cognitive, eating, sexual and somatic screens if relevant.

Depression — MSIGECAPS

LetterDomainScreening question
MMood"Sad, down or hopeless?"
SSleep"Too much, or too little?"
IInterest"Lost interest in things?"
GGuilt"Blaming yourself?"
EEnergy"How is your energy?"
CConcentration"How is your concentration?"
AAppetite"Appetite changed?"
PPsychomotor"Slowed, or restless?"
SSuicidality"Life isn't worth living?"

Nine letters mapping one-to-one onto the nine MDE criteria.

Mania — GST PAID

Mania is a distinct period of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy.

LetterItemScreening question
GGrandiosity"Unusually powerful?"
SSleep — decreased need"Less sleep, still energetic?"
TTalkativeness / pressured speech"Talking more than usual?"
PPleasurable risky activity"Overspending, risky driving?"
AActivity increase"Lots of new projects?"
IIdeas racing"Thoughts racing?"
DDistractibility"Distracted?"

Contrast to hold: the decreased need for sleep in mania (still energetic) is not the insomnia of depression (still tired), and mania's pressured speech pairs against depression's slowed speech.

Psychosis

Hallucinations are perceptual disturbances without an external stimulus; the screening qualifier is a voice nobody else can hear that is not your own voice.

Only auditory hallucinations point to a primary psychiatric illness. Auditory → schizophrenia. Visual → delirium and medical causes. Olfactory → medical, classically temporal lobe epilepsy. Tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Any modality other than auditory means look for a medical, neurological or withdrawal cause first.

Delusions are fixed false beliefs, in five types: persecutory (harassed, followed, spied on or harmed — paranoia) · grandiose (exceptional abilities, fame, a special mission) · referential (unrelated events or objects — TV, radio, signs — carry meaning aimed at the person) · erotomanic (someone of higher status is in love with the patient, often extending into a persecutory elaboration) · nihilistic (one is dead, does not exist, or the world has ended). The pairing to hold: nihilistic delusions point to severe psychotic depression, not schizophrenia.

Two delusion questions from the lecture
1. A 40-year-old woman with schizophrenia believes television commercials speak directly to her. Key: referential delusions.
2. A 64-year-old man says his body no longer exists, that he is dead and floating in a memory after the world ended. No key was ever given aloud for this one — on the definitions above it is a nihilistic delusion, inferred rather than stated.

Anxiety

Six conditions: generalized anxiety · panic · OCD · PTSD · social anxiety · specific phobias. The PTSD discriminator: symptoms after a frightening event are the norm and have resolved by a year out in about 90%; the roughly 10% still with nightmares, flashbacks and hyperarousal have PTSD. OCD and PTSD sit in separate DSM-5 categories.

5 · Substance use, past history, collateral

Substance use: alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, opioids, stimulants, hallucinogens, sedatives — then route, frequency, quantity, duration · last use and abstinence · withdrawal, tolerance, cravings · functional impact · past treatment · CAGE or AUDIT.

Withdrawal from CNS depressants can kill; opioid withdrawal does not. Alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates cause seizures, delirium tremens and death — management is diazepam plus thiamine, with admission for intravenous treatment. Opioid withdrawal is intensely uncomfortable but not lethal.

Past psychiatric history rests on four questions — admitted to hospital, suicide attempts, medications, psychotherapy? Family history covers depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, suicide, substance use; a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder confers about a 10% risk. Personal history spans early life, current circumstances, relationships and supports, identity and culture; collateral matters most in emergency psychiatry. And always think about a medical cause — sudden psychosis with a sky-high TSH is myxedema psychosis, treated with thyroid replacement.

6 · The Mental Status Exam — ASEPTIC

The MSE is the psychiatric equivalent of the physical examination, and its data are gathered throughout the interview — observational, not questions asked at the end. The descriptors are a vocabulary bank, not a checklist. A physical exam still matters — intoxication, withdrawal, side effects, movement disorders, catatonia, baseline weight and BP.

LetterDomainDescriptor vocabulary
AAppearance / behaviourapparent vs stated age · dress (inappropriate to weather or setting) · grooming · gait (slow, intoxicated, ataxic) · psychomotor activity (reduced, excessive) · level of consciousness (alert, confused, lethargic, stuporous) · abnormal movements (tics, tardive dyskinesia) · eye contact · attitude (cooperative, belligerent, submissive)
SSpeechrate (rapid, pressured, slowed) · rhythm (hesitant, rambling, halting, long pauses) · tone · volume · clarity · quantity (answers only, offers information, verbose)
EEmotion — mood and affectmood = subjective, what the patient reports · affect = observed · congruence · appropriateness · quality (euthymic, elevated, depressed, flat) · range (broad, restricted) · stability (fixed, labile)
PPerceptual disturbancehallucinations (auditory, visual, olfactory, tactile) · illusions = distortions of real images or sensations · depersonalization = they feel unreal · derealization = the world feels unreal
TThought process and contentprocess: circumstantial (answers eventually, after excessive detail) · tangential (never answers) · flight of ideas (rapid shifts, connections discernible) · loose associations (connections weak or absent) · thought blocking. Content: suicidal or homicidal ideation, delusions, obsessions
IInsight and judgementinsight = understanding of what is happening to them · judgement = using facts to make reasonable decisions (good, fair, impaired)
CCognitionorientation in three spheres (person, place, time) · attention · memory. Documentation line when not formally tested: "Cognition not formally assessed, but grossly intact."

Mood versus affect is the single highest-yield MSE distinction: mood is subjective, affect is objective — the patient says they are very sad but is laughing, so the affect is elevated or jovial. Quality, range and stability are three separate axes: flat is a quality, restricted is a range, and a question can turn on which axis a word belongs to. A depressed patient is expected to show restricted affect, which is why "broad affect" works as a distractor.

  • Insight and judgement dissociate and are scored separately: someone convinced they are Jesus Christ reincarnated has absent insight yet may behave appropriately, so judgement can be intact.
  • A patient responding to hallucinations is internally preoccupied, attending to internal stimuli; what cannot be observed is stated, never guessed — "gait was not observed".
  • Fast speech becomes pressured speech when it is hard to interrupt, cardinal for mania; in depression expect slowed speech, or speech latency.

7 · Challenges in the interview

  • Resistance — conscious or unconscious processes that interfere with the therapeutic objectives of treatment. Answer it with a process focus comment — "I notice you really don't want to talk about your relationships; what's going on there?" — which asks about the room rather than the material.
  • Transference — the patient imports feelings from past relationships, often childhood, onto the clinician as an authority figure, becoming angry, demanding or obsequious for reasons unrelated to you. Countertransference — the clinician reacting out of their own history: unusual anger, dread, boredom, acting out of character. Notice it, debrief, keep boundaries; the signal is deviation from your own baseline.
  • Learn the four together — transference = patient to clinician; countertransference = the clinician's own reaction; identification = loss of objectivity; therapeutic alliance = collaboration. And resistance blocks the material; acting out discharges it into behaviour.

8 · Diagnosis versus formulation

Diagnosis classifies against established criteria by symptoms, duration and severity, but does not explain why those symptoms occurred in this individual. Formulation is a hypothesis answering two questions: why has this patient fallen ill now, and what should we do to help. It must contain a "because". A 20-year-old and a 70-year-old can both meet criteria for panic disorder and be treated differently — in the older patient the panic may follow a stroke, in the younger it may be social embarrassment. The label is identical and the treatment is not.

9 · The 4 P's grid and the worked case

The grid crosses Bio | Psycho | Social columns (cultural factors fold into Social) against four rows: Predisposing — vulnerabilities raising risk (genetics, early life events, attachment insecurity); Precipitating — the trigger for onset; Perpetuating — what maintains it (substance use, avoidance); Protective — strengths that counteract the first three. The columns are the bio, psycho and social factors of the diathesis–stress model, so the grid is diathesis–stress with time added.

The case: a 25-year-old man with depression for three months after a relationship breakup. His mother had severe depression, was often hospitalized and unavailable as a parent; his parents divorced when he was 7. He has poorly controlled type I diabetes and cannot hold work because of frequent DKA admissions. He responded well to fluoxetine at 16, stopped six months ago because of cost.

BioSocialPsych
PredisposingFamily history of depression · type I diabetesMother's depression, often in hospital and away from him · father left when he was 7Insecure attachment, difficulty trusting · "I am not good enough"
PrecipitatingStopped the antidepressant because of costGirlfriend cheated on him → breakupReactivated inadequacy and mistrust
PerpetuatingPoor blood glucose controlLow income · social isolationOngoing conflict over trust and self-esteem
ProtectiveWilling to take medication, previously adherent, previous good SSRI responseGood healthcare teamPsychologically minded, self-reflective

What turns the table into a formulation: he is predisposed biologically by heritability and by type I diabetes as a risk factor for depression in its own right, through the inflammatory model. Socially, note the discipline — the same fact, the mother's depression, enters Bio as heritability and Social as absence. Psychologically, a child whose parent abandons him blames himself, which is where "I am not good enough" comes from, and the breakup reactivates it. That chain, plus a "because", makes it a formulation.

Placing a factor in the grid
Stem: a 36-year-old woman with persistent low mood feels isolated and struggles with close relationships; her parents were emotionally unavailable; she recently lost her job. Which is the psychological predisposing factor?
Key: the emotionally unavailable parents and the insecure attachment they produced — the only option both psychological and predisposing. Unemployment is precipitating, sleep disturbance perpetuating, passive suicidal ideation a feature of the depression, not a factor.

10 · Discriminators and exam traps

  • Circumstantial vs tangential — arrives eventually vs never arrives; flight of ideas keeps discernible connections, loose associations do not.
  • Hallucination vs illusion — no stimulus vs a distorted real one; depersonalization = self unreal, derealization = world unreal. Modality: auditory to schizophrenia, visual to delirium, olfactory to temporal lobe epilepsy, tactile to withdrawal. Nihilistic delusions — psychotic depression.
  • Transference vs countertransference — whose past relationship is imported. Resistance vs acting out — blocking vs discharging into behaviour. Withdrawal — CNS depressants can kill, opioids do not. Diagnosis vs formulation — a label names what, the grid answers why now, and placement questions turn on which cell a fact sits in.

One scoping note: Dr. Byrne said repeatedly that the 15-heading interview outline is not for memorizing now — it is reference material for the interview seminar. The concepts built on it — the MSE vocabulary, transference and countertransference, the 4 P's — are still fair game.

The interview is the cornerstone of assessment — safety, rapport, empathy. The MSE (ASEPTIC) is the mental physical exam, gathered throughout the interview rather than asked at the end. Diagnosis describes what; formulation — Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating, Protective across bio, psycho and social — explains why now, and the plan falls out of the columns: glycaemic control and restarting the SSRI, psychotherapy for self-esteem, the healthcare team against the isolation — not just "give him Prozac".

guides.title: Week 40 · 11 Treatment of Psychiatric Disorders (Byrne, Lecture 3)
guides.html:
Lecture 3 · Byrne

Treatment of Psychiatric Disorders (Byrne, Lecture 3)

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Biological, psychological and social treatments in psychiatry, mirroring the formulation grid: the seven psychotropic classes and the monoamine systems, drugs by disorder, ECT and neurostimulation, CAM and psychedelics, psychodynamic therapy and defence mechanisms, CBT and cognitive distortions, the DBT skills, and social, cultural and spiritual interventions.

The biopsychosocial treatment frame

Treatment categories mirror formulation categories one-for-one: biological risk factors get biological treatments, psychological factors get psychotherapy, social factors get social, cultural and spiritual interventions. Give a question a factor in one column and it can ask for the matching intervention in the same column. A psychiatrist works across all three: medication and ECT, trauma and group therapy, meditation skills.

Psychotropic medication classes

The seven classes are antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, anxiolytics, hypnotics (sedation and acute agitation), cognitive enhancers and stimulants. They are named for their primary application, which is not the same as their only one: antidepressants also treat anxiety, and antipsychotics also treat mood disorders and augment antidepressants in depression.

Monoamine systems

Monoamines — serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine — carry mood, cognition and behaviour, and most psychiatric medications work by modulating them. Their cell bodies sit in brainstem nuclei and project diffusely: of roughly 100 billion neurons only a few million are monoamine neurons, acting like switches for whole networks — hence broad effects and broad side-effect profiles.

MonoamineFunctionsNucleus of originTargeted by
Serotonin (5-HT)Mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, painRaphe nucleiSSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs
Norepinephrine (NE)Attention, arousal, mood, stressLocus coeruleusSNRIs, TCAs, bupropion, stimulants
Dopamine (DA)Reward, motivation, movement, psychosisMidbrain nucleiAntipsychotics, stimulants, bupropion

SNRI = serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor: it blocks both transporters, which is why it appears twice above. SSRIs are selective for serotonin alone.

Dopamine has a direction of dysfunction: high → psychosis, low → amotivation and anhedonia. Amphetamines raise it fast enough to cause paranoia and hallucinations; schizophrenia is too much dopamine in certain pathways, and antipsychotics lower it. Low-motivation depression and substance use behave like a low dopamine state — hence bupropion. The four pathways ("meso" = midbrain):

  1. Mesolimbic — emotion and reward
  2. Mesocortical — cognition and motivation
  3. Nigrostriatal — movement
  4. Tuberoinfundibular — prolactin regulation

Medications by disorder

IndicationAgents
DepressionSSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram); SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine); bupropion, mirtazapine, TCAs, MAOIs
Bipolar disorderLithium (mania, depression, suicide prevention), valproic acid (acute mania), carbamazepine, lamotrigine (bipolar depression); atypical antipsychotics acutely or for maintenance
Anxiety disordersSSRIs / SNRIs; benzodiazepines (lorazepam, clonazepam) short-term only — dependence; propranolol for performance anxiety
Psychotic disordersFirst-generation haloperidol; second-generation (atypical) risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine; treatment-resistant clozapine
ADHDStimulants methylphenidate, amphetamine salts; non-stimulants atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine
DementiaDonepezil (cholinesterase inhibitor); memantine (NMDA antagonist); antipsychotics cautiously for agitation
Alcohol use disorderAnticraving: naltrexone, acamprosate. Withdrawal: diazepam cover plus thiamine
Opioid use disorderMethadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist)

Dr. Byrne said plainly that the drug names are not to be memorized: stems give clues, so recognizing that fluoxetine is an antidepressant is enough. Recognition, not recall.

The unique pairings, and therefore the testable ones
lithium = the only agent for suicide prevention · lamotrigine = bipolar depression · valproic acid = acute mania · clozapine = treatment-resistant schizophrenia · propranolol = performance anxiety · methadone full vs buprenorphine partial agonist · anticraving is a different problem from withdrawal.

Neurostimulation

Brain stimulation uses electrical currents or magnetic fields to alter neuronal firing, and the split is anatomical. Transcranial (outside the skull): ECT, transcranial direct current stimulation, rTMS (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation — a coil on the scalp, no anaesthesia, no induced seizure) and magnetic seizure therapy. Surgical: cortical brain stimulation, deep brain stimulation (DBS), vagus nerve stimulation.

ECT, in practice
Electroconvulsive therapy is what it sounds like: a seizure is deliberately induced. An anaesthetist puts the patient under general anaesthesia, electrodes go on the outside of the head, the patient seizes while muscle relaxants limit its physical impact, and wakes a few minutes later. Dosing: 8–12 seizures, three times a week, over a few weeks. It is still the most effective antidepressant treatment available and is life-saving — the worked case was a psychotic depression with nihilistic delusions that had failed multiple medications.

DBS is neurosurgical: an electrode in the brain, connected to a small pulse generator under the skin like a cardiac pacemaker, for very treatment-resistant depression. The target is the subcallosal cingulate (Brodmann area 25), the white matter beneath the genu of the corpus callosum. Placement can be done with the patient awake, because the brain surface has no pain receptors.

Most effective is not first line. ECT is the most effective antidepressant treatment and neurostimulation is reserved for resistant cases — both at once. Recommending neurostimulation because one course of therapy failed is premature escalation and is keyed wrong. A stem mentioning general anaesthesia after failed medications and therapies points at ECT: you cannot seize an awake person.

Complementary and alternative medicine

CAM covers non-conventional approaches used alongside (complementary) or instead of (alternative) standard care, and several agents appear in mainstream guidelines. 30–50% of psychiatric patients use CAM, often without telling their clinician — which is why you ask. The slides name omega-3s and chamomile, while the lecturer also mentioned vitamin D and lavender; omega-3 for mild depression is the one both support. Be aware patients take these and will ask about them.

Psychedelics in psychiatry

Psychedelics alter perception, cognition and affect. Mechanism: 5-HT2A receptor agonism → disruption of default mode network activity → increased neuroplasticity and BDNF expression. Compounds: psilocybin, LSD, DMT, mescaline, ibogaine; MDMA and ketamine are often grouped here but are pharmacologically distinct (ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist). Under study in depression, PTSD and substance use disorders.

The default mode network monitors the internal state and is supposed to switch off to perform a task. In depression it stays overactive, and that is experienced as rumination. SSRIs and ketamine reduce that hyperactivity; psychedelics do it most intensively, close to a reboot.

Trials: two doses of psilocybin give a rapid, sustained reduction in major depression, and one session eases end-of-life distress for months; in phase 3 MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, 67% no longer met criteria at two months versus 32% on placebo. The governing conclusion: psychedelics are a catalyst for psychotherapeutic processes, not a standalone cure — set and setting is what turns a drug effect into a treatment.

Psychotherapy and validation

Psychotherapy is the intentional application of clinical methods and interpersonal stances derived from established psychological principles, to help people modify behaviour, cognition and emotion in directions the participants themselves deem desirable: it is not just talking, and the patient defines the goal.

Validation is the central skill — you cannot overdo it. What you think someone should do matters little; change comes from within them, and first you have to show them you understand they are suffering. "At least…" is the anti-validating move; "that sounds really hard" is the validating one.

Psychodynamic psychotherapy

  • Core idea: unconscious conflicts and early relationships shape current patterns.
  • Works through defences, transference and repetition of past relational patterns, focusing on self-awareness, emotional insight and the therapeutic relationship. Less structured than CBT; short-term or long-term.
  • Useful for chronic mood disorders, personality disorders and relational difficulties — a patient who feels abandoned explores how early parental neglect feeds a fear of rejection.

Defence mechanisms are unconscious strategies protecting against anxiety, conflict or distress. There are dozens; these five are the set to know.

DefenceDefinitionExample
DenialRefusing to accept realityInsisting they do not have cancer despite clear evidence
ProjectionAttributing your own thoughts or feelings to othersYou are angry and ask your partner why they are so angry
SublimationChannelling impulses into acceptable outletsAggression into sport; a long run after a breakup
DisplacementRedirecting emotion onto a safer targetCriticized at work, you snap at the family at home
RegressionReverting to earlier developmental behaviourActing like your twelve-year-old self at a family dinner

The list is not ranked, but levels differ: denial and projection are primitive, regression and displacement neurotic, and sublimation is mature — as are humour, altruism, anticipation and suppression.

Cognitive behaviour therapy

  • Identify and challenge automatic thoughts, with homework, goal setting, behavioural experiments and relaxation training; practical and time-limited.
  • Panic disorder is treated with CBT: the patient recognizes catastrophic thoughts ("I'm dying") and tests them through interoceptive exposure.
  • The CBT triangle: thoughts, feelings and behaviours joined by bidirectional arrows between every pair — changing behaviour changes thoughts, not only the reverse.

Psychotherapy produces measurable brain change, and the pattern differs from medication — CBT and antidepressant-facilitated recovery move the same regions in opposite directions. The regions are not the examinable part; the principle is that psychotherapy is not fluffy.

Cognitive restructuring is spotting the distortion inside an automatic thought and testing it against reality.

DistortionDefinitionExample
All-or-nothing thinkingBlack-and-white thinking"If I'm not perfect I have failed"
Over-generalizingA broad pattern from a single event"Nothing good ever happens"
Mental filterAttending only to certain evidenceNoticing every failure and none of the successes
Disqualifying the positiveDiscounting good outcomes"That doesn't count"
Jumping to conclusionsMind reading and fortune telling"Nobody spoke to me, so they hated it"; "I for sure failed that exam"
Magnification and minimizationCatastrophizing, or shrinking something inappropriately"Fail the exam → kicked out → no rent → homeless" — the chain is the giveaway

Distortions form because stress pushes us to simplify reality to reduce anxiety — briefly effective, worse over time. The intervention starts with naming the pattern as a pattern.

Skills: the physiological sigh, TIPP and the body scan

The physiological sigh is two inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale through the mouth: the biggest inhale you have taken all day, another sip of air at the top, then a long slow exhale through pursed lips — at least 10 seconds. It is called physiological because it is what a child's body does on its own when settling.

Why a slow exhale calms you, in order
Anxiety is the sympathetic nervous system on overdrive. A slow exhale reduces intrathoracic pressure, changing venous return, which lowers heart rate and blood pressure. That drop signals up through the brainstem to the limbic system that everything is fine, and only then does the prefrontal cortex come back online so cognitive techniques can work. The order matters: the body settles first, then the thinking works — the common mechanism behind every skill here.
Breathing exercises are not risk-free. Three physiological sighs can drop heart rate by 15–20 beats per minute, and a participant in a meditation group fainted when her blood pressure fell too far. Teach it seated, and practise before an exam or a talk rather than somewhere a faint would matter.

Third-wave therapies focus on acceptance, mindfulness and values-driven behaviour, and on changing your relationship with thoughts rather than the thoughts themselves — the contrast with classical CBT.

DBT (dialectical behaviour therapy) teaches four modules — emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness — from dialectical philosophy, Buddhism and behaviour therapy, and is especially effective in borderline personality disorder. ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy) accepts painful experience while committing to action aligned with personal values; no indication was named.

TIPP is DBT's crisis-survival set: reduce physical arousal, tipping body chemistry from sympathetic to parasympathetic.

  • T — Temperature: ice pack on the back of the neck or cold water on the face, recruiting the bradycardic diving reflex.
  • I — Intense exercise: ten jumping jacks is enough.
  • P — Progressive muscle relaxation: a five-second squeeze and release per group — fists, shoulders, legs, then all three.
  • P — Paced breathing: exhale longer than inhale; the physiological sigh is this limb.

The body scan is the relaxation-training skill: quiet place → deep breaths → slow the thoughts → start at one end of the body → move part by part → come back into the room. Two instructions carry it: non-judgement and non-striving, and returning attention to the body whenever you notice you are distracted.

Social interventions

Social determinants — economic stability, education, health care access, neighbourhood, social and community context — are strongly linked to psychiatric outcomes. Social interventions are not adjuncts but essential components of effective psychiatric care. Know the four categories, not the named programmes.

  • Case management — assertive community treatment, intensive case management.
  • Supportive housing — Housing First, rent subsidies, shelter.
  • Income support — disability benefits, medical leave.
  • Peer support — peer mentors and lived-experience programs.

Cultural and spiritual considerations

  • Explanatory models — ask "What do you think is happening?" rather than assuming your own model applies.
  • Language barriers — use trained interpreters, never family members. Racism, migration stress and poverty worsen illness.
  • Spiritual screen — Do you have spiritual or religious beliefs? Do they help you cope? Positives: community, meaning, lower suicide risk. Negatives: guilt, feeling punished, conflict with medical advice.
  • Practical issues — Ramadan fasting means adjusting medication timing; Halal, Kosher or vegetarian diets mean checking pill ingredients; First Nations, Inuit and Metis patients may want traditional healing with or without Western care.

Approach all of it with cultural humility: be respectful, ask, and collaborate.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • ECT vs DBS: ECT requires general anaesthesia; DBS electrodes can be placed awake, so an anaesthesia clue points to ECT.
  • Antidepressant transmitters: norepinephrine and serotonin, even though three monoamines are taught; dopamine is the antipsychotic and stimulant axis.
  • Therapy vignettes are read from what the sessions do: childhood → psychodynamic; thought records and worksheets → CBT.
  • Two meanings of ACT: acceptance and commitment therapy vs assertive community treatment.
  • Anticraving is not withdrawal: naltrexone and acamprosate reduce craving; diazepam with thiamine covers withdrawal.
  • Dopamine pathways: prolactin tuberoinfundibular, movement nigrostriatal, reward mesolimbic, cognition mesocortical.
  • Social answers bring the service to the patient — assertive community treatment and housing, not another appointment.
Biological, psychological and social treatments are the same three columns as the formulation grid. Know the monoamine map, the unique pairings (lithium and suicide prevention, lamotrigine and bipolar depression, clozapine and treatment resistance), that ECT is the most effective antidepressant treatment yet reserved for resistant cases and needs anaesthesia, that psychodynamic therapy looks backward while CBT tests thoughts, and that every skill works by dropping heart rate so the prefrontal cortex can come back online.

Integration · CBL · WFQ

Week 40 Integrated Review: CBL 40 and WFQ Walkthrough

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

CBL 40 (Stanley) question by question with Group 8's unvalidated draft and the cultural formulation grid, all 17 WFQ questions walked through against the official key, and Dr. Byrne's own statements about what is and isn't testable.

The weekly formative quiz, question by question

The quiz prints 17 questions, numbered from 4 and skipping 7 and 8; Q1, Q2, Q3, Q7 and Q8 appear in neither the paper nor the key, so those five topics are simply missing. The printed numbering is used throughout.

Q4 · Military psychiatry in the world wars. Which statement about military psychiatrists in the two wars is true? → they used hypnosis as one of their interventions. Shell shock was first described by Charles Myers. Their primary role was rapid return to duty, not long-term quality of life, and hysteria and shell shock were never fully connected.

Q5 · The DSM paradigm shift. Which edition is widely considered the turning point in psychiatric nosology? → DSM-III (1980), which introduced operationalized criteria and an atheoretical, descriptive approach. DSM-I and DSM-II were narrative; DSM-IV was an update, not a shift.

Q6 · Degeneration. Degeneration theory rests on which assumption? → some humans carry traits that make them less suited to modern society. Inherited defects were held to render people unfit for contemporary life; the theory fed eugenics and ended in therapeutic nihilism, so "mental illness is treatable" is its opposite.

Q9 · Overdose, borderline personality disorder, and the request to admit. A 24-year-old woman with BPD is medically stabilized after an acetaminophen overdose and the emergency physician asks you to admit her. → assess her current mental state and suicidality. Admitting, discharging, or declaring she does not need admission are all inappropriate without assessment.

The half-truth trap. It is true that many patients with chronic, fluctuating suicidal ideation do not benefit from admission — but saying so before assessing is the error the question is built around. Risk assessment always precedes disposition.

Q10 · Idealization and devaluation. A 28-year-old woman with BPD calls her boyfriend the best person in the world one week and the worst the next. Which criterion is this? → unstable relationships. What fluctuates is her perception of another person, not her self-image or her mood; anger, unstable identity and affective instability are real criteria that do not fit this vignette.

Q11 · Which list is BPD? → the set of nine: affective instability, suicidal behaviour, inappropriate anger, relationship instability, unstable sense of self, fear of abandonment, impulsivity, dissociation or paranoia, emptiness — threshold ≥ 5 of 9. The wrong lists smuggle in neighbours: shallow emotion and over-read intimacy (histrionic); envy and exploitation (narcissistic); reckless disregard for safety and aggressiveness (antisocial).

Q12 · What turns symptoms into a disorder? A 30-year-old woman has six weeks of sadness, insomnia and poor concentration after a layoff, is struggling at work and in relationships, and has intermittent suicidal thoughts. → her low mood is affecting her interpersonal functioning. Clinically significant functional impairment is the dividing line from a normal emotional response — not the stressor, not the duration, not a comorbid history.

Q13 · Four of nine. A 28-year-old man has low mood, poor appetite and amotivation with clear work and social impairment, but meets only 4 of 9 criteria, so no major depressive episode is diagnosed. → arbitrary cutoffs can exclude clinically significant cases. The distractors invert reality: categorical systems are the rigid ones, they do define symptom clusters, and comorbidity is common. The four stated limitations: arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity, subthreshold illness.

Q14 · Evolutionary psychology and anxiety. A 22-year-old student with persistent worry about deadlines asks why he feels this way when nothing bad is happening. → such traits were once adaptive in ancestral environments. Modern stressors activate the same alarm systems with no physical threat present; a disorder arises when the response becomes dysregulated.

Q15 · Mental status findings in depression. A 36-year-old man, sad for two months, cannot get out of bed, has stopped working and playing guitar, has no appetite, and believes his family would be better off without him. → slowed speech. Expect poor eye contact, psychomotor slowing and reduced speech output. Broad affect is the opposite of the restricted or blunted affect expected; grandiose delusions belong to mania or psychosis, since delusions in depression are mood congruent (nihilistic, somatic, guilty); and concentration is impaired, not intact.

Q16 · Transference. A patient in a severe depressive episode becomes unusually deferential toward the clerk and repeatedly seeks reassurance, later revealing abandonment by paternal figures. → transference. Learn the four together: transference, the patient redirecting feelings from past relationships onto the clinician; countertransference, the clinician's own reaction; identification, loss of objectivity; therapeutic alliance, the collaborative working relationship.

Q17 · Cultural engagement. A 23-year-old refugee with hypervigilance, nightmares and avoidance is hesitant about Western psychiatric care and believes his distress comes from ancestral spirits. → explore his explanatory model of illness and book a follow-up. Understanding the explanatory model builds trust and shapes culturally sensitive care; challenging the belief is its exact opposite. The same principle governs the interview, along with using trained interpreters rather than family.

Q18 · Medication hesitancy. A 36-year-old woman with low mood, anhedonia and early morning awakening has had three months of psychotherapy with little improvement and fears medication side effects. → explore her concerns about pharmacologic options. Hesitancy is an invitation to inform and decide together — not to coerce, and not to escalate prematurely to neurostimulation or inpatient care. The plan must also be feasible.

Q19 · Antidepressant targets. A 35-year-old man is started on medication for moderate major depressive disorder; which neurotransmitters are most affected? → norepinephrine and serotonin, the monoamines tied to mood regulation and the target of most first-line agents.

Read that distractor closely. Dopamine is a monoamine and is taught alongside serotonin and norepinephrine. The option "dopamine and glutamate" is wrong because of glutamate — not because dopamine does not belong.

Q20 · Prevalence in adolescence. A parent asks how common mental health disorders are in a 13-year-old. → 20%, or 1 in 5 youth, most often anxiety, ADHD and depression. The adult numbers taught this week: roughly 50% of the population by age 40, and suicide accounting for 24% of deaths at ages 15–24 and 16% at ages 25–44.

Q21 · Commonest diagnosis in children and teens. → anxiety disorders — most prevalent, often unrecognized, prone to worsen untreated, and responsive to early intervention.

Q22 · Temperament. Which best describes it? → innate traits influencing early interaction with the world: present from infancy, biologically based, and foundational to personality. Decode the distractors — a stable pattern developed through experience is character or learned behaviour; enduring traits deviating from social norms describe a personality disorder; an emotional bond with a caregiver is attachment.

Topic map and answer string

QTopicKeyQTopicKey
4Shell shock, hypnosis, return to dutyC15Mental status exam in depressionC
5DSM-III as the paradigm shiftC16Transference vs the other three termsC
6Degeneration and eugenicsC17Explanatory model, cultural careA
9Assess risk before dispositionC18Medication hesitancy, shared decisionsD
10Idealization equals unstable relationshipsC19Monoamine targetsC
11BPD criteria set, ≥ 5 of 9A201 in 5 youthD
12Functional impairment defines disorderB21Anxiety commonest in youthC
13Arbitrary categorical thresholdsC22Temperament vs character vs attachmentB
14Evolution and anxietyC

Answer string: 4 C · 5 C · 6 C · 9 C · 10 C · 11 A · 12 B · 13 C · 14 C · 15 C · 16 C · 17 A · 18 D · 19 C · 20 D · 21 C · 22 B.

The case-based session — Stanley, a refugee claimant with trauma

Stanley is a refugee claimant with a hearing coming up, persecuted in relation to his sexual orientation. He survived severe interpersonal violence in which his mother was killed, sustained a shoulder injury, and was forced to migrate, losing his home and occupation. He sleeps poorly, carries guilt and self-blame, fears return, and faces housing and financial insecurity; a supportive cousin, employment and education sit on the protective side. He seems closed off early in the encounter and later discloses suicidal ideation. The supervisor is unsure between PTSD and adjustment disorder, suggests psychiatry, and wants medical causes excluded meanwhile. Q1, Q5, Q9 and Q12 are submitted individually by 8 am on the day of the faculty-led session; the rest are group work.

#The questionWhat a good answer contains
1What do you want to know about his refugee status?Where the claim stands and when the hearing is; health coverage and OHIP eligibility; supports he already has
2Communication considerations before meeting himLanguage and a trained interpreter; trauma-informed care; cultural difference approached without assumptions
3The patient who seems closed offName confidentiality explicitly; a private, safe setting; unhurried pace; your own body language, tone and attitude
4Responding empathically once he disclosesAcknowledge and validate, thank him for trusting you, check how he is feeling now, ask what he needs before continuing
5What the DSM has said about homosexualityA disorder in DSM-I and DSM-II; removed by vote in 1973; replaced by "sexual orientation disturbance", then "ego-dystonic homosexuality" in DSM-III, dropped in DSM-III-R. Hooker's projective-test study of 30 gay men against matched controls found no difference
6The next step after disclosed suicidal ideationAssess directly, now. Drivers; timing and what makes it better or worse; plan, intent, means and access; past attempts; certainty and hopefulness; protective factors; a safety plan
7History-taking with a refugee patientThe history of presenting illness is taken the same way; then add migration and pre-migration experience, losses, legal status, language and supports
8Biological, psychological, social and cultural factorsThe formulation grid below
9PTSD or adjustment disorder; excluding medical causesBasic screening bloodwork, complete blood count and TSH among them, before settling on a psychiatric label
10Community and interdisciplinary supportsSettlement agencies; refugee lawyer or legal aid; social work, Ontario Works, housing; primary care and refugee clinics; LGBTQ+-affirming organizations; culturally appropriate mental health care. The letter for the hearing is the piece most often left out
11Supports available in this sessionWhat you can set in motion today: a named organization, a referral, a follow-up booked before he leaves
12Advocacy organizations in the GTAEquitable health care, housing and income supports; have specific names ready rather than categories
13Making sense of his symptoms and next stepsThe formulation's because, followed by a plan: risk, medical exclusion, referral, supports
14Does trauma require a DSM diagnosis? The pros and cons of labellingTurns on what a diagnosis is for — access, coverage, shared language — against stigma and a label displacing the social context
15How trauma affects identity and relationshipsAsked deliberately without reference to diagnosis: answer from trust, safety and self-concept, not from criteria

Two model lines for Q4: "You went through something terrifying, and you lost your mother in the middle of it. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me — how are you feeling talking about this now?" and "Is there anything you need from me right now before we continue?"

The formulation grid

The chart is the familiar four P's — predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective — against biological, psychological and social columns, with a cultural column added. Worked through for Stanley:

BiologicalPsychologicalSocialCultural
PredisposingNo clear biological vulnerability identifiedLongstanding fear tied to concealing his sexualityChronic threat of discovery or persecutionSevere stigma and criminalization of sexual orientation where he lived
PrecipitatingShoulder injury and pain from the attackGrief after his mother's death; guilt and self-blame; fear of returnViolent attack; forced migration; loss of home and occupation; the upcoming hearingPersecution for his orientation; displacement from his community
PerpetuatingPoor sleep; persistent painTrauma reminders; guilt; anticipatory fear of returnHousing instability; financial insecurity; few supports; legal uncertaintyIsolation from community; unfamiliar systems; discrimination
ProtectiveNo medical comorbidity or substance useFuture orientation; help-seeking; perseveranceSupportive cousin; employment; education; engaged with health careLGBTQ+-affirming community and legal protection in Canada

These entries are a study group's draft, not a tutor key — use the grid as a model of the shape of a formulation and expect the faculty session to move cells and add more. The narrative matters as much: his distress is unfolding while his right to remain is unresolved, which is what makes the threat of return feel immediate.

What is and is not testable

Dr. Byrne was explicit about scope for each piece of the week.

MaterialHer guidance
Introduction to nosology moduleDo not open it — no questions come from it
History of psychiatry moduleLook at it; there might be a question — interesting and not heavy
Introduction to psychiatry readingTwo pages, very general, nothing to memorize
Personality-disorder modules 7 to 11Do look at these — the pre-reads for the workshop, which is wasted time without them
The case-based sessionNo preparation needed — show up and do your best
DSM-5 category tableBe familiar with the main categories
Panic disorder criteriaNot to be memorized — shown to convey what DSM criteria look like
The interview deck and its 15-heading outlineHeavy, for reference; revisited in the seminar
Monoamine chemical structuresNot to be memorized
Drug namesNot all of them, but know that fluoxetine is an antidepressant — questions will give clues
Neurostimulation detail and the deep brain stimulation videoDetail not needed; the video not testable
Complementary and alternative agentsNot the agents themselves, but be aware patients take them and will ask
Psychotherapy definitions and psychodynamic detailFor psychodynamic, only that it is less structured, short or long term
The neuroimaging slide on CBTNot the brain areas — the point is that psychotherapy also changes the brain
Social interventions tableOnly the bolded section
What "you do not need to memorize" actually means
Every one of those lines is about rote recall as printed — none says the concept is off the exam. This week's quiz tested the symptom threshold, mental status vocabulary, the monoamine targets and the four P's despite the disclaimers. Read it as you will be given clues, not asked to regurgitate, never as "skip it".

Discriminators and traps

  • Disclosed suicidal ideation → direct risk assessment first — not a referral, not an admission decision, and never a generalization about patients with BPD.
  • Functional impairment is what converts symptoms into a disorder — not the stressor, not the duration, not a comorbid history.
  • 4 of 9 is not a major depressive episode and 5 of 9 is — the standing illustration of an arbitrary threshold.
  • Idealization and devaluation are about other people, so they score unstable relationships, not unstable self-image.
  • Explore the explanatory model; never challenge the belief — and interpret through a trained interpreter, not a relative.
  • Medication hesitancy is an invitation to explore, not to escalate.
  • Exclude medical causes before settling between PTSD and adjustment disorder.
Two habits carry the whole week: assess before you decide — risk before disposition, medical causes before a psychiatric label — and explain before you diagnose, giving the formulation's "because" rather than only the DSM's "what".
